I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice and I regret I have been unable to give him notice of this question because the matter has just come to my attention. The question is as follows. In view of the report of the restrictive trade practices commission concerning the production, purchase and sale

of flue-cured tobacco in Ontario, and in view of the fact that on April 1 next a vote is being taken amongst tobacco growers in Ontario for the purpose of deciding whether or not the growers should come under the jurisdiction of the Ontario farm products marketing board, is there any action the minister can take to assure that the funds and records of the flue-cured tobacco marketing association will not be used or misused to influence the vote in favour of the flue-cured tobacco marketing association?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if my hon. friend planned not to give notice of his question he certainly produced a very complicated one of which he gave no notice. Offhand my impression is that the matter which he raises is the responsibility of the provincial attorney general of Ontario.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. In view of the recommendations of the report, does the minister not consider that his department has a direct interest in the present situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT
speechtext: I do not apprehend that any recommendation in the report gives me authority to invade a field of activity which is provincial.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT
speechtext: Order. I suggest to hon. members that they cut down a bit on the length of the foundation for their questions.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Justice a supplementary question. Since the minister is somewhat uncertain as to the situation, would he be good enough to look into the matter right away and see if there is anything his department can do, as I am informed there is fear among the growers that the funds and records of the present association are being used to influence the vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT

maintopic: LIVESTOCK
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice, whom I seldom crossexamine. In view of the fact that the acting minister of agriculture in British Columbia, Kenneth Kiernan, moved in the British

Columbia legislature an amendment to a motion concerning humane slaughter of animals, which urged that the government of Canada amend the Criminal Code to prohibit slaughter of food animals in packing houses without stunning prior to bleeding, and is reported as stating that anything other than federal legislation would be just an expression of pious opinion and would not accomplish what is wished, would the minister consider such an amendment to the Criminal Code?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: LIVESTOCK
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
The minister is always prepared to consider any amendment to any federal statute which will produce beneficial results. But I do not think in the present case an amendment is required. Section 387 (l)(a) of the Criminal Code reads as follows:
387. (1) Everyone commits an offence who
(a) wilfully causes or, being the owner, wilfully permits to be caused unnecessary pain, suffering or injury to an animal or bird, . . .
I think before we consider changing that provision we should have some demonstration that it has been invoked and has been found to be wanting in such a set of circumstances as that to which my hon. friend's question refers.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. In view of the dissatisfaction of a considerable number of Indians of the Caughnawaga reserve over the offers of settlement made for the lands taken over from them for the St. Lawrence seaway, will the government consider the setting up of a claims commission in order to settle those claims and numerous other claims of Indians across Canada in regard to their property rights in what they own and do not own?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a relatively small minority of those persons who have an interest in property on the Caughnawaga reserve who have not yet made settlement with the St. Lawrence seaway authority for the lands that have been taken over for the seaway. They were assured from the outset that if they were not satisfied with the compensation which was offered by the seaway authority and which, after very careful consideration by independent experts, was accepted by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, any individual
Inquiries of the Ministry case could be referred to the exchequer court for adjudication. It seems to me that that puts these people on a basis at least equal to that of any other persons whose property is being taken, and it would, I think, be quite wrong to substitute for the accepted procedure for settlement of expropriation cases a procedure that was somewhat different. Indeed, I would think, sir, in view of the fact that this offer was made, it might be construed as being a reflection upon the exchequer court, which I would not want to have any part in making.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration a question supplementary to the one asked by the hon. member for Calgary North. He spoke of independent appraisers. Could the minister tell the house who engaged the independent appraisers with regard to the Caughnawaga reserve property?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not know which of my officials may have advised me as to whom to engage but I engaged the appraisers.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext: That is the point in which I was interested. They were employees of your department?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext:
No, they are not employees of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, because they are in the business of appraising; but they were engaged and contracted with by my department.
I think it is highly commendable, sir, that hon. members on both sides of the house are anxious, as we are, to see that these Indians get a fair deal. As there is some misunderstanding perhaps I should say that the seaway had its appraisers and we had our appraisers. I, as minister, have taken the view that my first duty was to be fair to the Indians and I have not agreed to any settlement that was not recommended to me by the appraisers we engaged.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext:
Could I ask
another supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Was it true that there was at least one appraiser who acted on behalf of both the department and the St. Lawrence seaway authority?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext: Not to my knowledge, sir, and I do not think that could have happened.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a further question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration supplementary to the question

Inquiries of the Ministry asked by the hon. member for Nanaimo. I should like to have the minister explain to the house how it is that officers of his department are making offers on behalf of the St. Lawrence seaway authority to members of the Caughnawaga Indian band.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext:
What happened is that the St. Lawrence seaway authority expropriated this property for a specific purpose and I believe under the law it is the responsibility of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to satisfy himself that the compensation is adequate. When in our negotiations with the seaway authority we reached the point where we thought that what they were then willing to pay was adequate, an officer of my department discussed the matter with the Indians. We felt that it would be a rather ridiculous thing to have an officer of the seaway, without much detailed knowledge of conditions on the reserve, spending his time discussing these matters with the Indians.
In every piece of property on the reserve there is a band interest, that is the interest of all the Indians living on the reserve and having the right to live on the reserve, and in most cases also there is the individual interest of an individual Indian. Compensation is being paid both for the band interest and the individual interest.
Once we had come to the conclusion that what the seaway was willing to pay in a particular case seemed to us to be adequate compensation for the individual Indian, then we felt it would be better for our officers to carry on negotiations with the individual Indians. I took the position, and I have taken it repeatedly with the president of the seaway authority, that I could not agree to any over-all figure for the compensation until all the individual claims were satisfied.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext:
Just one further question,
if I may. Earlier the minister made some reference to the use of the exchequer court. Could he explain what advice has been given to the Indians by the department in regard to going to the exchequer court if they are not satisfied with the offers being made by the seaway authority?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext:
Any band council, any
members of a band or any individual concerned knows because he or they have been told that if he or they are not satisfied the department will do whatever it can to facilitate a reference to the court. It may be possible that no action can be taken in the ordinary sense, but whether that is so or not, the government has given an undertaking to facilitate a reference to the court

for the purpose of determining what is appropriate compensation for the individual interests. All hon. members know that an Indian does not have title in the sense that a freeholder has and there is a band interest as well as an individual interest to be considered which complicates the whole business.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext:
Perhaps this matter could
be pursued on some other occasion. We have had several questions on this matter now.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext: I should like to direct a further question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. Do the minister and/or his legal advisers consider there is a right of expropriation as far as Indian reserves or Indian lands are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext: That matter has recently been adjudicated upon by the high court in the province of Quebec. I believe notice of appeal has been given, and it would be very presumptuous on my part to give an opinion on a subject before the appeal court-the court of Queen's bench, I believe it is called- in the province of Quebec.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext: May I ask the minister what position the Indian affairs branch has taken on this matter up to date?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext: Of course the hon. gentleman is a member of parliament just as I am and he took part, whether he supported it or voted against it, in the passing of a bill at the last regular session of parliament, I think it was, to confirm this very right. However, it has been questioned whether parliament had the right to pass that legislation-

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext: That is the very point.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY CAUGHNAWAGA INDIAN RESERVE    REQUEST FOR SETTING UP OF CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext: -and that question is before the court. It would certainly be very presumptuous on my part to express any opinion on a matter before the courts.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: IMMIGRATION
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration whether any plans exist to assist with their transportation Canadian residents of the United Kingdom who are anxious to return to Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minisler of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
Well, sir, an amendment was made last year, I believe, to the Appropriation Act in one or other of my estimates-I am speaking from memory and I cannot be sure which one it was-which inserted the word "settlers" as well as "immigrants", and that was done precisely for the purpose of making it possible to give assisted passage loans to Canadian citizens who had
Inquiries of the Ministry ceased to live in Canada but who had not given up their citizenship and who wished to come back to settle in this country. Of course, it would not be the practice to give assisted passage loans to Canadians who had gone to England or to some other country in the last year or two, and, having been a failure as emigrants, decided they would like to get their passage back to Canada; but there are a great many people who went- not a great many, perhaps, but a good number-20 or 30 years ago, particularly before the war when times were pretty rough in some parts of Canada, and particularly before 1935-

maintopic: IMMIGRATION
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
Now that times have
changed they are rather anxious to come back to Canada and we felt it was desirable to give them every opportunity we could.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION
speechtext: Might I ask a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I am thinking particularly of those cases of men who served during the second world war and who for one reason or another-perhaps marriage- decided to remain in the United Kingdom but who now feel that they would like to return to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: IMMIGRATION
speechtext: Oh, they would certainly be covered.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION
speechtext: They would be covered?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: IMMIGRATION

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize contributions to be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund to provinces in respect of costs incurred by them in providing insured hospital and diagnostic services pursuant to provincial law and to agreements made in accordance with the said measure, to commence when at least six provinces, containing at least half the population of Canada, have entered into such agreements and qualified for the receipt of such contributions.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution is based on the government's offer to the provinces on hospital insurance and diagnostic services as announced on January 26 last by the Prime Minister. I should like now briefly to summarize the federal government's proposals in the following manner.
First of all, the government declared its willingness to assist with technical support and financial assistance any province wishing to embark upon agreed phases of provincially administered health insurance schemes involving no constitutional change or interference with provincial affairs as soon as a majority of provincial governments representing a majority of the Canadian people indicated their readiness to proceed. Since the opinions expressed by the provincial authorities at the conference on the question of priorities confirmed fully the view of the federal government expressed by the Prime Minister at a meeting held with the provinces on October 3, 1955, the government gave priority of attention in its offer to the development of plans to cover diagnostic services and hospital care. The government declared as well its readiness, once a majority of governments representing a majority of the people of Canada declared that they were ready to introduce hospital insurance, to recommend to parliament that it provide by legislation grants to cover a share of the cost of this element of health insurance to take effect when that majority of provinces have such plans in operation.
I should like to note that it will be apparent now from the wording of the resolution to which I now speak and from the text of the bill when it is before the house that a favourable modification has been made in the original requirement that a majority of

provinces must have their plans in actual operation. It should also be noted that the government has not waited until six provinces have declared their readiness to proceed but has proceeded in advance of its commitment a year ago to introduce legislation at a time when one additional province is needed to make up the required majority.
The federal offer stipulated that provincial hospital insurance plans, in order to qualify, should make coverage universally available to all persons in the province, include provision of specified diagnostic, laboratory or radiological services to persons in hospital and within an agreed time to persons outside of hospital; and provide for a limit to be placed on co-insurance or deterrent charges so as to ensure that an excessive financial burden will not be placed on patients in respect of hospitalization costs at the time of receipt of service.
Mr. Chairman, the federal government went on to propose that its contribution to the cost of hospitalization provided for under a recognized provincial hospital insurance plan would be a specified proportion of shareable costs and these would be determined on the basis of normal operating and maintenance costs for certain standard ward care, and provide for certain exclusions. Costs would be shared by the federal government not only with respect to care in active treatment or general hospitals but also with respect to care in chronic and convalescent hospitals. Furthermore, the federal government would share in the costs of treating and caring for tubercular and mental patients in general hospitals.
The federal contribution in respect of each recognized provincial plan would be based on the following formula, applied to shareable costs as already defined: first, 25 per cent of the annual per capita costs for hospital services in Canada as a whole and, second, 25 per cent of the annual per capita costs in the province itself multiplied by the population covered. This formula takes into account the fact that hospital costs vary greatly from one province to another and also that some provinces have greater financial resources than have others. By basing contributions in part on the national rather than the actual provincial average the formula is weighted in favour of the less wealthy provinces, particularly the maritimes, whose available financial resources might otherwise make it difficult for them to provide the services which are possible in the better-off provinces.
In that portion of the formula which involves paying 25 per cent of the actual shareable costs in each province, recognition is

given to the position of the higher cost provinces, namely British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Ontario. In that portion of the formula which involves paying 25 per cent of the national average, recognition in the government's formula is given to the position of the lower cost provinces, particularly the maritime provinces which, incidentally, are also for the most part those provinces with similar financial resources from which to provide their smaller share of the cost.
That is in general an outline of the proposal which the federal government has made to the provinces and in respect of which five provincial governments have signified their concurrence in principle acknowledging in so doing that their schemes in being or in the planning stage come within the four corners of the proposal which was first announced to parliament last January.
I am sure the house will recall the day when the former prime minister, the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, on May 14, 1948, announced to this house and through this house to the nation the national health grants program. I venture to remind the house of what he said on that occasion, for the words which he then used have not, in the intervening years, been far from my mind or from the mind, the judgment and the consideration of the government as a whole. Mr. King pointed out then that the grants provided important financial assistance to the provinces in the development of better health services for the people of Canada wherever they might live. But their true significance and purpose, he emphasized, went far beyond that; they were, in fact-and I quote the exact words he used at that time-"a fundamental prerequisite of a nation-wide system of health insurance". Ever since that time, Mr. Chairman, this government has kept-as have others-that concept of the purpose and goal of the national health program in the forefront of its thinking and planning. We have laid the groundwork for what is now being done. We have planned, stimulated and financed, in collaboration with the provinces, the expansion and development of our local public health services, our skilled health personnel, our hospital plant and equipment, to meet the requirements of our growing population.
This foundation has involved federal expenditures of over $200 million, and also substantial expenditures by provincial governments and by voluntary organizations all over the country. As a result of this program, in communities all across our country, hundreds of new hospitals have been built to better serve the health needs of the people. Improved care has been made possible for
Health Insurance
the victims of cancer, tuberculosis, mental illness and so on. Progress in medical research has been greatly speeded up. The children of Canada have been given the protection of the Salk polio vaccine, as a result of the joint efforts of the two senior levels of government. These and other developments have helped to bring the nation's health services to a most desirable level and to set the stage for the hospital insurance legislation we are now seeking to introduce.
In all these years we have constantly reminded members of this house, the governments of the various provinces, and indeed the Canadian people of our longer range objectives. We have sought to enlist enough of the provinces in support of our objective to take the step envisaged in the original plan. Now, after this period of careful and responsible preparation, in co-operation with the health departments of the provincial governments, through the national health program, we are ready. We are now, I believe, with confidence, in sight of our long-sought goal. One more province is required to make up the needed majority representing the majority of the people of our country to make our program of hospital insurance a reality.
Now, sir, the basic objective of the federal hospital insurance proposal is to provide, in co-operation with the provinces, protection for all Canadians against the possibility of heavy or unexpected hospital expenses. An important by-product of the program, moreover, will be to put the nation's hospitals, again in co-operation with the provinces who will have the responsibility of administration, on a much sounder financial footing. It is in the confident hope that not just one but several more provinces will indicate shortly, I trust, their intention to proceed that I am now presenting to the committee this resolution under which we are seeking the necessary authority to introduce legislation which will make possible the realization of a nationwide system of hospital care insurance in Canada.
I need say little about the resolution, nor would it be in order for me at this juncture to point out the details of the contents of the bill whose introduction we seek through this resolution. It will be sufficient, I think, to state that the bill will embody and implement the full intent of the federal government's proposals as presented by the Prime Minister last January. It will neither require, nor indeed countenance, federal interference in provincial affairs. It will fully respect and safeguard provincial autonomy and jurisdiction. It will leave undisturbed the constitutional relationships of the various levels of government, and requires no constitutional

Health Insurance
amendments. It will authorize the conclusion of agreements with provincial governments desirous of embarking upon provincial programs of hospital insurance and diagnostic services; and will provide the authority necessary for the payment of substantial federal contributions in accordance with the terms of these agreements.
It will require that coverage under provincial hospital insurance plans be universally available without arbitrary exclusion, artificial residence or other barriers or discrimination of any kind, to all persons in the province. This will include Indians, Eskimos or other groups of persons who might otherwise be excluded by statute or on grounds of provincial policy from participation in provincial hospital insurance programs. It will provide for the determination of shareable costs, and for the exclusion therefrom of certain items which are not shareable by the federal government. The details of these items I have already given before the estimates committee which sat during the course of the last session of parliament. The bill will embody the formula for sharing costs, based partly on the national experience and partly on the actual provincial experience, which has already been set forth in the offer which I outlined a few moments ago.
For all provinces, taken as a whole, the federal contribution will amount to 50 per cent of those costs defined as shareable, while for each province the federal contribution will amount to 25 per cent of the per capita shareable cost for the nation as a whole, plus 25 per cent of the per capita shareable costs for the province itself, multiplied by the population covered in the province. Finally, Mr. Chairman, the bill will define the nature of the benefits to be provided under approved provincial hospital insurance plans, including bed care on the public ward level, without any arbitrary restriction as to the number of days, the usual hospitalization extras, out-patient and diagnostic services as may be agreed upon.
The resolution makes clear, of course, the requirement that six provinces, representing at least half of the population of Canada, must have passed the necessary provincial legislation; concluded agreements; established the required provincial administrative machinery and otherwise qualified for the receipt of contributions before the federal obligation under any of the agreements becomes effective. This is not, of course, inconsistent, with the general proposal which was announced to the house by the Prime Minister, but modifies in some degree the

more detailed proposal which I discussed with the ministers representing the ten provincial governments.

speechtext:
Now, Mr. Chairman, presentation of this resolution is, I am sure, for all of us in this house an historic occasion.
I wonder if I may say, without criticism, that in all the years I have been in this house I have had no greater feeling of satisfaction than at this very moment. Never has the government, and I am sure others in this house, had such a feeling of complete conviction as to the vital importance of the legislative action we are now proposing the terms of which, in its financial implications, must be considered as imposing added responsibilities on the people of Canada who will be called upon to accept the decision of this parliament. I can say that the government has never felt more completely certain that the good that will flow from an act of this parliament will be understood and appreciated and valued in the years to come by the people of this country.
We are witnessing today, in the presentation of this resolution, the culmination of much effort and much study; the work of countless persons in this house and in this country; and the collaboration of many governments, federal as well as provincial. All of them, government and individuals alike, have been imbued, in my judgment, with a common determination to find some means of bringing improved health and hospital services to our people, to ensure the availability of skilled hospital and diagnostic services when required, to spread more equitably the financial burden of expensive hospital care.
I know this problem can only be reached and solved by co-operation between the two senior levels of government. It cannot be done on any other basis and preserve the traditional constitutional and administrative patterns in our country. And so we have reached the end of the period of preparation and preliminary planning. We are now ready to move along a new highroad of progress, a highroad which leads to the assurance of better, more adequate health and hospital services, whenever they are needed, for the people of Canada.
I take my seat with the words of a great Canadian citizen, those of Laurier, who said:
The fight of democracy for freedom, for equality of opportunity and for substantial justice to all individuals still goes on. Canadian politics still has its greatest work to do; the welfare of the common man at the common task is its first consideration.

Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I express the hope that in the spirit of these noble and moving words of a great Canadian prime minister, every member of this house, regardless of party, will support this resolution which can mean so much to the people of this great nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution before the house reads:
That It is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize contributions to be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund to provinces in respect of costs incurred by them in providing insured hospital and diagnostic services pursuant to provincial law and to agreements made in accordance with the said measure, to commence when at least six provinces, containing at least half the population of Canada, have entered into such agreements and qualified for the receipt of such contributions.
I have read this resolution into the record, sir, in order to point out that this is a measure for insuring hospital and diagnostic services. That is a point on which I wish hon. members to be quite clear. We have been aware for some time that negotiations have been proceeding between the government of the province of Ontario and the federal government to bring such a plan into effect and I am proud that Ontario has taken such a forward step to bring such an agreement to the present point where at last we can visualize a hospital insurance plan for Canada. It has been a long road since 1919 when the Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, as leader of the Liberal party, promised health insurance for Canada. From 1919 to 1948 covers a period of 28 years since health grants were first introduced. To the health grants we gladly assented, and today we have before us the present resolution for the introduction of hospital insurance.
For the past 12 years, on behalf of the Conservative party, I have advocated measures to benefit health conditions and care for the people of Canada. All political parties in this house have been in favour of such a measure. We may not all have agreed on the general form of insurance, but one point is clear, and that is that we all appreciate the fact that the public money that is spent on legislation to combat sickness, disease and misery, will pay high dividends in health standards and happiness of the people of our nation.
Sir, I wish to quote from the closing paragraph of a book written in 1945 by Henry E. Sigerist, professor of the history of medicine in the Johns Hopkins University.
The problem of financing such health services is secondary. More difficult economic problems have been solved. We have all the money we need when we are attacked by a ruthless enemy. Disease is also an enemy. Its attack may be less spectacular but is just as pernicious as any that occurs in actual warfare, and we certainly can find
Health Insurance
the comparatively small funds required to fight this war to a victorious end. The health and welfare of every individual is the concern of society, and human solidarity beyond the boundaries of nationality, race and creed, is a true criterion of civilization.
This is a measure for health insurance. Throughout the ages, in the attempt to combat disease and sickness, there were generally evolved special types of structures, and chief among those structures was the hospital. I bring this in because it shows how hospitals first came into being. In the early centuries of our era it was a guest house that provided shelter for the indigent and the stranger and later became a place where the indigent sick were nursed and received free medical treatment. When medical science progressed, giving rise to aseptic surgery, and to better diagnostic methods, the hospital was no longer a place of death, but the source of all medical activities sought by the rich and poor. From the few rooms that were then maintained for the sick, in the early medieval monastery, the hospital developed into the large wards of the middle ages. As the development progressed it became the highly complex institution of our present day with large and small sick rooms, solariums, operating rooms, laboratories and facilities for medical research. The modern hospital has lost the gloom of the earlier eras where every feature reminded one of the proximity of death. Today the modern hospital remains a place of suffering and disease but the accent is on life.
I have previously pointed out in this house, not later than last year, that the matter of keeping well is of the utmost importance. This particularly applies in the present agreements to the diagnostic feature. A few hundred years ago, in European history, the point of view among those interested in the healing arts was concerned with the curing of disease. At this point I wish to point out that there is a great deal of difference between curing and using preventive measures. Preventive measures were almost unknown at that time. The most they hoped for was to have physicians sufficiently versed in the understanding of disease that sick people under their care would rapidly recover.
Under conditions such as these it becomes clear that only a small proportion of the population shared in the benefits of the increasing skill of the physicians; but under present conditions, hospitals, laboratories and physicians are in close contact with new scientific equipment. Today physicians are armed with new drugs, advanced methods of treatment, and methods which would have

Health Insurance
been considered unbelievable in the previous centuries. Today curing is not sufficient. The problem today is not only to get people well but to keep them well. If we were still to pursue the old idea of keeping people well by curing disease it would be a costly and expensive proposition from the taxpayer's point of view. We must also pay particular attention to prevention. From year to year we are making progress in the campaign to keep people well. When I spoke on this last year on the health estimates I said that one could even now visualize a period in the future when the needs for hospitals would diminish owing to the great objective of full preventive measures rather than the older concept of curing disease.
In our consideration of health measures we must note the fact that while illness creates suffering it is also an economic loss. The sick man cannot work and therefore he loses his wages. Sickness may disable a worker for long periods of time. Then, if in addition to his loss of wages he is faced with a heavy hospital bill he is placed in a position of financial hazard.
While many diseases can be prevented, many can be cured in the initial stages by early treatment. This is the point where diagnostic methods and hospital care become very important, and the phrase "diagnostic methods" assumes importance in relation to the resolution. But the hospital, which plays an increasing part in all aspects of medical care, has been forced to raise its costs considerably. Medical supplies, drugs and appliances are not only more expensive but are needed in rapidly growing quantities.
At this point I should like to remind hon. members that while new treatments are often expensive the duration of stay in hospital has been markedly cut down and earlier cures effected by their application. Nevertheless, new drugs, new methods and the cost of hospitalization present a financial burden with which the average citizen finds it difficult to cope.

It may be difficult to estimate the risk of sickness for the individual but it can be estimated for large groups and therefore in order to spread the risk among a number of people the principle of insurance must be applied.

The federal government has not recognized mental patients in the present agreements under discussion. It does agree to the inclusion of these mental patients while in general hospitals. The problem of mentally ill patients is one of our greatest problems. Owing to advanced methods of treatment it must be pointed out that the length of stay in hospital has been steadily

cut down in the past 20 years, enabling the hospital to care for more patients. However, to make full progress there must be general recognition of the fact that mental illness is a form of disease comparable to any other disease which affects the human body. In 1934 patients discharged from mental hospitals had a stay of 5.4 months in comparison with 1954 when the stay was 1.8 months. The point to be noted is that in 1954 three patients could be treated in the bed required to accommodate one patient in 1934. Mental health clinics, private physicians and out-patient departments of general hospitals are giving an increasing amount of treatment for this disease. But the fact remains that the 1954 statistics indicate there were over 68,000 patients in mental institutions in Canada. This number exceeds by 10,000 the number of patients in public hospitals.
While the health grants have assisted in this matter, I cannot but feel that this is one of our foremost problems in the field of national health and should receive further consideration in these agreements in order that it can be dealt with more adequately. This fact must be recognized. According to the statistics of the Canada Year Book, of the 68,157 patients on the books of mental institutions at the end of 1954, 62,323 were in hospital. This is 87 per cent more than the 33,290 reported in hospital at the end of 1932.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution placed before the committee today by the Minister of National Health and Welfare deals with a matter which is of equal if not greater importance than any subject which could be dealt with by a legislative body in this country. It deals with the health of our people and proposes a forward step in social concern for that health. Therefore we shall support the resolution. I shall indicate the features in this proposal which appeal to us and which we think are good, but it will also be necessary for me perhaps even to a greater degree to refer to the features in respect of which we think the resolution falls short.
We welcome in particular the proposal of the government that the services to be provided under this resolution shall be universally available in the provinces in which this measure becomes effective. There have been some discussions during recent weeks as to the meaning of universality, but I dare to believe that whatever differences there may be between the government of Canada and the government of Ontario regarding universality those differences relate only to the time as to when full universality will be realized.
I dare to believe that there is agreement between the two governments to which I have referred, as well as on the part of all the other governments that are in on discussions of this matter, that sooner or later, but sooner rather than later, the services provided under any hospital scheme must be available to every resident of the province concerned. In our view no social program in the health field is worth its salt unless it is based on the principle of universality, and we welcome that important aspect of this legislation.
We also welcome the fact that the legislation provides for a proportion of the costs of the services covered by this legislation to

be paid for out of the general revenues of the federal treasury. I shall have something to say later about the percentage proposed in the resolution, but at the moment I am dealing with the good points of the matter and I say that we welcome the fact that a proportion of these costs is to be paid for out of the consolidated revenue fund of the federal government.
The reason we welcome that feature is that we feel that health care-indeed, we go a lot further than the hospital care covered in this resolution-is something that should be paid for by the people of Canada according to their ability to pay rather than according to their particular need of health or hospital care. Any program of health insurance or hospital insurance that requires people to pay for it on a fixed premium basis, if you are dealing with it nationally, or that requires people to pay for it on a basis that is related to the amount of care that they receive, violates that principle. But when you pay for a portion of health or hospital care out of the consolidated revenue fund you are drawing on those funds of the nation which are acquired mainly through corporation and income taxes and they are the funds that most nearly approximate the principle of paying according to ability to pay.
It will be obvious from what I am saying that we feel that the percentage of hospital care to be paid for out of the consolidated revenue fund should be much higher than the 50 per cent indicated in this legislation, but we welcome the fact that the government has gone at least that far. We welcome the fact that the government realizes that the day has come in Canada when a considerable portion of the health care of our people, as reflected in their hospital costs, should be paid for not according to the particular need of the individual who has to be hospitalized but according to the ability of the people of Canada to pay. Those are the two features of the legislation which we welcome the most, its universality and its recognition in part of the desirability of health care being paid for according to ability to pay.
When the minister was speaking I made a note of an additional point to welcome but as he got a little farther along in his remarks I found I had to cross out the note. At this moment I am not just sure where we stand with respect to the matter he knows I have in mind, but perhaps it will be cleared up before the discussion in committee has been concluded. The minister said early in his remarks that a change was to be made in that part of the statement made by the Prime Minister in January, 1956, and indeed there would be a change in the corresponding part of this
Health Insurance
resolution, that referred to the necessity of having the six provincial plans in operation before payment could be made to any of the provinces.
I dared to hope from what the minister said when he first referred to this matter that a modification was being forecast which would make it possible, once the required number of provinces had agreed to establish their plans, for payment to be made to those provinces which have their plans in operation without having to wait for all six plans to be in actual operation. Something the minister said later suggested that I had gone too far in my understanding of the modification because he said later that no province would draw any money until all of the provinces were in a position to draw the money simultaneously.
I regret very much that the change forecast in the legislation in that respect is not more substantial than it seems to be. We feel very strongly that the whole formula that the government has laid down is not a good one. We think that its requirement that there be six provinces representing a majority of the population of Canada before anything is done is too stringent a requirement. As we have tried to point out a number of times already in this session, there are now five provinces that have agreed and the population of those five provinces represents over 56 per cent of the population of Canada. We feel that the spirit of the suggestion made by the Prime Minister in January, 1956, has been met and that the government should now modify the requirement that six provinces must agree before anything is done.
The minister will say that the government has modified its position to some extent in that it is now introducing this legislation even though only five provinces have indicated their agreement but, although he has introduced the legislation, right in the resolution itself is the requirement that six provinces agree and that six provinces have their plans in operation before the operation as a whole can come into effect. We feel that this is a mistake.

I concede the government's right to stipulate before it brings in legislation that any proposed legislation will not be brought in until certain terms satisfactory to the government have been met, but I suggest to the government that it is not good practice to include in an actual law to be placed upon our statute books what amounts to a right to any one province of the country to veto legislation passed by the parliament of Canada.
It is understood according to the British North America Act that once an act has been passed by the House of Commons and the Senate and has been given assent in the name of the Queen by the Governor General the legislation is in effect and I submit that it is not proper for any such legislation passed by the three branches of parliament to have in it a provision that keeps that legislation from coming into effect by virtue of a veto of some-indeed of even ore-of the provincial governments. Once the government has come this far and is prepared to lay legislation of this kind before parliament, once it is satisfied that it has virtual agreement from enough of the provinces, I think there should be no inclusion of that kind of a formula in the legislation itself. Once the legislation has been passed and given assent it should be clear that it is the law of the land so far as Canada is concerned.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare says this is an historic occasion. One would expect him to say that. No. We are getting just a mere portion of that promise, namely a proposal to finance hospital insurance, and even that only to a limited extent.
Since the historic nature of this occasion has been referred to by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, I might just take a moment to invite hon. members to read the debate on this resolution that took place at the Liberal convention in August, 1919. It was moved by Mr. King and seconded by Mr. Arthur Roebuck who is now a member of the other place. There were two other speakers, namely the late Hon. George P. Graham and Mr. D. D. McKenzie.
It is a very interesting debate. The resolution was a lengthy one under the general heading of "Labour and Industrial Conditions". There were in all some 20 points to it, including the commitment with respect to sickness insurance. But to my disappointment I find that of the four speakers whose speeches occupied 20 pages in the record of that convention, not one of them referred to this question of health insurance at all. They put it on the record, passed it and let it lie there. Most of those who spoke to this comprehensive resolution, which included a promise of sickness insurance, spoke primarily to the last paragraph in the resolution that was then before the convention, which was a paragraph that promised that the Liberals would do their best to restore the control of the executive by parliament and to restore parliamentary responsibility to the people of Canada.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
