maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is evidence to indicate that the minister is anxious to have the committee pass this resolution so that the bill based upon it might be introduced. We feel that probably we shall be in a much better position to discuss it at the bill stage, and for that reason I do not intend to occupy very much time.
I listened to the minister this afternoon waxing eloquent in his usual fashion and obviously without too much effort. He demonstrated an extremely high degree of

Health Insurance
enthusiasm, which caused him to use such expressions as this being a memorable day, and being an historic occasion. In fact, at one stage I almost thought he was going to shed tears but he did not. It was obvious, too, upon this occasion, as upon previous occasions-whether it was intentional or not- that the minister was endeavouring in some way or another to create the impression in the minds of certain people in certain places that this was the first step in the field of health insurance. In fact, I was thinking back to those times when the federal government granted assistance to the provinces to help them carry out responsibilities in the field of health where it was in their jurisdiction to do so, and I could not but conclude that there is not a single solitary field where the federal government has finally agreed to make grants that at least certain provincial governments have not themselves blazed the trail, pioneered, and suffered ail the headaches that go with this sort of thing.
We have already had references to the hospital insurance scheme in Saskatchewan, for example, to the one in British Columbia and to ours in Alberta. They have been operating under such plans for a considerable period of time and now, as far as they are concerned, the federal government has come along, dragging its feet as usual, and has now proposed a plan under which assistance will be granted to the provinces to enable them to bear the burdens which some of them have borne for some time and to enable other provinces which have not yet ventured into this field to do something for their people. I just said that to remind the committee that the real pioneering in connection with these things has been done by the provinces in co-operation with the municipal governments with voluntary help, with organizations, and so on, and not by the federal government at all.
We heartily endorse the basic principle of this resolution, Mr. Chairman, namely, that the federal government should assist the provinces in this field of health insurance. As I say, we support the basic principle included in the resolution. We heartily approve of the fact that the administration is to remain on the local level in the sense that the provincial governments will conduct the work of administration. We have stated upon many occasions that whatever is done in this federal field by the provinces and the federal government-in most cases the municipalities enter into it- the administration should remain on the local level. I think this is a particularly good feature of this proposal. We feel that every effort possible should be made, particularly in this field of health, to avoid

unnecessary, and what I would call most undesirable, centralization of administration.
We have not at any time, Mr. Chairman, urged the federal government to plunge in all at one time in a hasty fashion, in a showy fashion, for political purposes, on an allembracing, comprehensive national health insurance scheme.
I personally feel that while there seems to be a good deal of tardiness at times, it is better to lay a good solid foundation with respect to any of these matters and build on those good solid foundations. By that I am not suggesting for a moment that certain of these things could not have been done prior to this time; but we do feel that it is wise to proceed carefully-I will not use the word "slowly"-and cautiously, and not by ill-advised leaps which some would seem to want us to do.
I think, too, it is extremely important that while we are considering treatment we should never at any time forget to assist in the field of prevention. I am vitally concerned about legislation of this kind, Mr. Chairman, particularly because of the fact that it becomes more obvious every day that the Canadian people are finding it more and more difficult, if not impossible, in so many cases, to secure and pay for hospital, medical, dental, optical and other services, and to pay for the drugs which so many of them have to purchase because of illness. It must be obvious that not only are families becoming impoverished as a consequence of illness involving hospitals, and so on, but there is ample evidence that that very thing has happened to a good many families already. One reason why it is becoming increasingly difficult for people to meet these costs is the fact that almost every day the cost of everything is going up; almost every day we find the tax burden, no matter at what level of government, becoming more oppressive, leaving less and less all the time for the individual to pay his own way, as it were. Many families are being left without sufficient with which to purchase the necessities of life, thereby creating a condition, involuntarily, of course, where health deteriorates as a consequence. It almost has a double-barrel effect; it is almost a vicious circle. I sometimes wonder where we are going eventually to arrive.
As I said a moment ago, on the one hand government spending increases by leaps and bounds; taxation increases by leaps and bounds; and living costs are going up by leaps and bounds. Citizens are left with less and less, which results in more and more help being required from the government and more government assistance, leading people

to be more and more dependent upon the government. That makes me wonder. Of course, as they become more and more dependent on the government they become more and more subject to government regulation. I wonder perhaps if this is not the sort of thing which my leader had in mind in 1953 when I recall his saying that a grave danger facing us is a tax dictatorship.
This situation results, as I said earlier, from a vicious combination of factors. I do not want it to be taken from that comment that one can in any sense be opposed to the principle of the resolution now before us, but it is a side thought to which I have devoted a great deal of attention. This appears to be a vicious circle and one wonders where we are going to eventually land in this whole scheme.
As far as that amendment is concerned we cannot at this point understand why it is the government is so insistent upon waiting until a certain number of provinces have signed up, as it were, before bringing into operation the proposal contained in this resolution.
It has been intimated that the five provinces which have already indicated agreement represent more than 50 per cent of the population and that rather limits the value of the statement made by the minister only a short time ago. I do not remember the exact words he used but his statement was to the effect that they were not asking the minority to pay for the costs-no, that was not it. Perhaps the minister could repeat the statement for us?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Yes. What I said was that the policy enunciated by the Prime Minister and repeated by me in the estimates committee when I met with the provincial ministers was that the federal government was not prepared to recommend a policy that would result in the payment by the taxpayers of Canada of financial assistance in the matter of hospital insurance to a group who represent in the broad context of the over-all plan a minority in the nation.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: A minority of the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: No, a minority of the people. Well, a minority of the provinces, yes. And may I say, by the way, that view was supported by the minister of health for Alberta and others at the conference.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: It would appear that whether or not he agrees that he is, what the minister is talking about is a majority of the provinces and not a majority of the population because we already have five provinces in which we have a majority of population.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
Fifty-six per cent.
Health Insurance

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
Yes, 56 per cent. It is small wonder that some of us are confused with respect to this. However, in the course of considering the bill itself we may clear up some of the confusion and receive information in answer to the questions which are in our minds.
There is one other matter I am wondering about. I am interested in knowing if it is the intention, when and if the agreement of six provinces is obtained, to make this proposition apply in the same way in each of the six provinces. I have a reason for asking about this.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Do you mean the insurance scheme itself?

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Yes. I want to know if the same rules and regulations will apply in one province as in another.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Do you mean that the schemes, must be the same?

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Yes. Whatever plan we endorse here, is it to be applied in each of the six provinces in the same way?

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Perhaps in order to understand my hon. friend's question I may be permitted to ask this. Does he mean that in order to come within the purport of this broad proposal each province must have the same kind of insurance scheme?

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: No. Let me give you an illustration of what I mean. When the federal Disabled Persons Act came into operation there were two provinces in Canada which already had their own schemes.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Yes, precisely.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
I refer, of course, to the province of Alberta and the province of Ontario; but they were not treated in the same way. I understand that all the people who qualified under Ontario's disabled persons act were immediately permitted to come under the federal scheme but each case was reviewed later on and if following the examination of a particular case by the board of review it was found that the recipient of the disabled persons pension did not qualify under the federal regulations then that person was dropped from the role, but during the period of time which elapsed while they were attempting to determine his eligibility under the federal scheme the central government paid.
In Alberta they did not do that as far as I can learn. In Alberta they had to establish the fact that a person receiving a disabled pension under the act of that province could qualify under the federal act before he was

Health Insurance
brought in under the federal act, the difference being that for a period of months the Alberta government had to continue paying a pension to certain disabled persons who were qualified to come under the federal act but who had not proven that they possessed the qualifications because a board of review cannot handle these things overnight while in Ontario, as far as I am aware, a different situation obtained.
That is the sort of thing I have in mind. I am not suggesting that any two provinces should have exactly the same scheme. That could not be expected particularly where you have provinces with differing schemes operating at the present time. What I am anxious to see is that whatever we pass here each of the participating provinces will get the same kind of deal, if I may use that expression. I am interested in seeing that we secure fairness.
I notice that the minister gives me a rather strange look but I cannot believe he does not know what I mean regardless of how I may have complicated my question in expressing it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: I do not understand, really. When we get into a discussion of the bill perhaps this can be cleared up. We are certainly going to treat all the provinces fairly. I sincerely do not quite understand the hon. member's question but when we get into discussion of the bill perhaps my hon. friend can illustrate his point to make it more clear.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: My point is this. Let me put it this way. If the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan happen to participate in the scheme there will not be one set of rules for one province and another set for the others?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: I can give my hon. friend that assurance.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: I shall have a few more questions to ask when we reach the discussion of the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Thank you.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister in his very histrionic speech-I have not yet seen him more so-said this was an historic occasion. Well it certainly is. This is the occasion when we celebrate the end of 38 years of promises by the Liberal government concerning health insurance. For the last eight elections we have seen this same government bring out the subject of health insurance, dust it off, promise it, wait until the election was over, wrap it up in cellophane again, place it back on the shelf marked "E" for elections, and wait for

another election to come along. But two years ago, Mr. Chairman, a very statesmanlike gentleman in this country, Premier Leslie Frost of Ontario, decided that this Liberal dishonesty should come to an end and so, to the great dismay of the Liberal government, he demanded that the question of hospital insurance be placed on the agenda of the dominion-provincial conference to be held in October 1955.
The Liberal government, of course, was dismayed and disconcerted by this prospect because they were planning to use the subject of health insurance as bait for the ninth successive election; to promise it again, and tell the people that if they voted the government in they would have health insurance. Of course the government had no more intention of bringing in a health insurance plan following the ninth election than they had in the case of any of the eight previous occasions.
However, Mr. Frost is not a man to be fooled with. He was very determined, and demanded that this question be placed on the agenda of the conference, and this was done. The other provincial premiers were very glad that this was done, and thought it was a good thing that Mr. Frost had taken an adamant stand in this matter. The question of a health insurance plan was well received at that conference, with the result that in January of the following year, 1956, a three-day conference was held on the subject of health insurance. Following that conference the Minister of National Health and Welfare made a statement in section 4 of which he said:
Provincial hospital insurance plans, in order to qualify for consideration, should:
(a) make coverage universally available to all persons in the province.
Further on in that statement the minister referred to certain costs in which the federal government would not share, including capital costs-for example, depreciation, interest, amortization of debentures, etc.- and provincial administrative costs and the cost of caring for mental or tubercular patients.
Mr. Frost agreed with the requirement of the federal government that coverage should be universally available, as stated by the minister. He and his health department thought they could get a coverage of 85 to 90 per cent, or higher if possible. It is to the advantage of any province to get the highest possible coverage, because the higher the coverage, the lower the unit cost to the province.
That is obvious, because when a plan like this comes into operation, those who tend to stay out are the young and healthy, the

ones who cannot see a need for hospital insurance for some time to come, while the ones who enter first are those who need hospital care and will thus constitute the greatest drain on the province's resources. So it is to the advantage of a province to get as high a coverage as possible, and that is what Ontario intends to do.
Mr. Frost and his government disagreed with the unwillingness of the federal government to participate in capital costs, administrative costs, and the cost of caring for tubercular and mental patients. They contended quite rightly that administrative costs are very much a cost of any plan, and that you cannot have a plan without administrative costs. You also cannot have any kind of a plan without capital costs, as you must rebuild your institutions, provide new machinery and equipment and so on from time to time. Administrative costs are very much a part of the cost of your plan. The Ontario government also feel that two very important categories of treatment today are those affecting mental and tubercular patients. They feel, I think quite rightly, that those costs should be shared by the federal government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: I know my hon. friend would not want to give a wrong impression to the Canadian people on a matter of such importance. Tubercular and mental patients, as the hon. member for Lanark mentioned, who are in general hospitals are being taken care of. I am sure the hon. member is not arguing that we should use a hospital insurance plan to subsidize provincial governments. A hospital insurance plan is intended to subsidize individuals in connection with their hospital costs.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: It is a question of whether the federal government is willing to assist the provincial governments in caring for tubercular and mental patients. I think it is most desirable.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: So do I. My hon. friend knows that will be done under the national health program.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
I hope it will; I am glad to have the minister's assurance that it will be done. Mr. Frost is an easy person to get along with, and he was most co-operative and ready to do anything to help this federal hospital insurance plan get under way. Therefore he said that until the federal government saw its way clear to agreeing to share these additional costs, which he believed should be shared, the provincial government would continue to pay the full amount. To use his own words, he fitted his plan into the four corners of the requirements laid down by the minister in January
Health Insurance
of 1956, and which were expressed in the statement he made following the conference. That was all very well until January of this year, when it seems the minister suddenly realized that he was going to have five or six provinces agreeing, and the plan would soon be put into operation. Things were probably moving a little too fast to suit him, so he then decided that instead of the coverage being universal, the coverage should be 100 per cent of the people in the province.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Who said that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: My hon. friend of course is badly informed on this subject.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Then the minister had better get that straightened away with Mr. Frost, because that is certainly the impression you conveyed to him and his ministers.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Has my hon. friend read the correspondence between the premier and myself? I am sure if he rereads it he will want to correct that impression.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
I read it very carefully, and it was certainly my impression and the impression of officials of the Ontario government that the minister was putting a serious block in the way of this plan becoming a reality. However, Mr. Frost persuaded him that this requirement of 100 per cent coverage would be very costly and would require coercive methods in order to make it work. If there are people who do not want to come into a plan you have to use coercive methods to force them to come in, and that is a very costly thing to do. However, once again, thank heavens, Mr. Frost was able to persuade the minister of the error of his ways, and the minister finally came to agreement with the province of Ontario on the details of the plan that would be put into operation.
The only block seems to be that a sixth province is required. Why that requirement was ever brought into the negotiations I do not think any person can understand.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
Would you like me to explain
right away?

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
If we had not insisted on a sixth province we would not have five now. I would ask my hon. friend to give very careful consideration to this. What we are after is a nation-wide system. If you just have a program which says it will apply to any province that wants to come in, you would not get any more than the five we have now. If my hon. friend is sincere in trying to promote a nation-wide system, then let him not argue against this essential condition of having six

Health Insurance
provinces. If we insist on six, we will get six or even seven, and if we insist only on five that is all we will have.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: How do you know?

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
That is the strangest bit of
arithmetic I have ever listened to. If we have six we will have seven, but if we do not require six we will not have any, or some such nonsense. The provinces which have come in have done so, not because of any requirement on this government's part but because they wanted to come in, because the great majority of the people in this country want a hospital insurance plan. That is the reason the provinces which have already come in have done so. I do not think there is any logic in the minister's statement that if you require six you will get seven. It sounds like some kind of shell game.
This seems to be just one more difficulty being placed in the way of this plan coming into operation. You have five provinces, and for heaven's sake realize that those five provinces are in because they want to come in. If a sixth province wants to come in it will come in because it wants to, not because of the minister requiring it to.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: We will sign with the five provinces as soon as the legislation is passed.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Will the legislation be passed before the sixth province comes in?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: If my hon. friend will help to pass this bill, the minute it does pass we will sign with the five provinces.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: And start the plan immediately?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: I did not say that.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: How soon will you start the plan?

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: My hon. friend has read my speech. I said when the six provinces passed the necessary legislation and had agreements in being and had their acts in force. My hon. friend knows that if we are not beginning until January 7, 1959, that is not the fault of this government.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: I still cannot see any logic in requiring six instead of five. Why not pick seven; why not pick four? How did you arrive at six? Can you tell me that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: I have already explained it.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, it seems that the minister just does not want to make sense. I do not think his statement that the requiring of a certain number makes the thing more desirable or less desirable adds up. I will simply conclude by saying that as far as I can see the people of Canada owe a very great debt to Premier Frost for being
(Mr. Martin.]
the prime mover in all this. If it had not been for the fact that he demanded that hospital insurance be placed on the agenda of the dominion-provincial conference in October, 1955, we would not have this legislation before us today.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Why did not Premier Frost bring in a provincial plan?

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: That is exactly what he is in the process of doing.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
Why did he not do it
before?

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
So, Mr. Chairman, I think perhaps this plan could be called the Frost plan, because if it had not been for him we would not have it before us today. If it had not been for his foresight and determination, and his desire to see a measure like this put into operation, it is certain that we would not be debating it at this moment.
I end by urging the minister to waive this silly requirement of six provinces. Take five provinces, sign them up and let us get the whole matter under way without further ado.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question. Can we agree on one thing? Is it not a fact that the premier he is talking about so much noticed the need of health insurance when he felt the pressure of public opinion in his own province?

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Mr. Frost does what he feels is good for the people of his province. He wants health insurance.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Under pressure.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: He is doing everything to force its adoption.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: When pressure is brought upon him by the people.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: No, not at all. He is the one who is bringing pressure on the federal government to make good on the promises that were made over 38 years ago.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have a few brief words, because in 1937 I had a resolution on the order paper with respect to health insurance.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Who pressed whom into action now?

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: I spent two years on a committee under the chairmanship of the late Right Hon. Ian Mackenzie. We were ready with our bill but something happened and we could not get it across.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Still Liberal promises.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
Some said at that time that we did not have the co-operation of the provinces. Whether or not they were asked I do not know, but we did not get the bill through. Now we have the bill and it is not state medicine. I think the medical associations all over Canada will appreciate that it is not state medicine. It is a hospital plan. It does not interfere with the doctors. The patient can choose his own doctor, and I expect that the doctor can charge his fee in the usual way.
It has been said that the Liberals have been terribly slow in bringing in the bill. We know it is a law of nature that things that grow fast do not abide, whereas things that grow slowly and steadily do abide. After this slow growth over long years we now have a bill that the opposition supports up to a certain point. I congratulate the minister on the way he has stuck to his job. I congratulated him once before when he wiped out all the different nationalities in Canada and made us all Canadians, not Irish Canadians, not Scotch Canadians. Now we have him sticking to his task and bringing in this legislation after hard and faithful toil. Some people criticize him for being slow but they never tell him that he is lazy. They dare not do that, because he might step across the floor of the house to prove that he is not.
I congratulate the minister on bringing in the resolution at this time, and I am looking forward to seeing the bill. I may have some criticism too, but as I see it now this is a job well done. Stick to it, Honourable Paul.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is apparent that the hon. member for Fort William is very easily satisfied. The Minister of National Health and Welfare boasted of the expenditures which have been made in the field of health. He has spent something over $200 million. May I remind him that his colleague the Minister of Defence Production has spent more than that on the development of the CF-105. He spent more than that on the mid-Canada radar line.
It has been admitted that the federal authority has some responsibility in this field of health, but I think the present resolution is quite inadequate. Indeed, I find that the speech of the minister does not hold out as much help as the green book proposals of the government of 1945. On page 28 I read the following:
Although great progress has been made In Canada during the first half of this century, there still remains a tremendous job to be done in improving the national health and in extending the benefits of modern science and medical care to all parts of the nation and all sections of the population.
If that was true 12 years ago it is even truer today. At that time the federal authorities were able to take some credit for the
Health Insurance
fact that the tuberculosis death rate had been reduced from 200 per 100,000 at the beginning of the century to 48 in 1944, and I am quite prepared to admit that there has been a substantial drop since 1944. But at that time the federal government did indicate that they were interested in the fight against tuberculosis. At that time they went on to point out in the green book:
There are great inequalities in the quantity and quality of health care available to different groups of Canadians, and in the costs of such public and private health services and medical and hospital facilities as are now available.
I also read the following:
Nearly all countries have adopted health insurance in one form or another. The chief exceptions to date have been Canada, Australia and the United States . . .
Then the federal authorities outlined some of the advantages that would accrue to the nation as the result of having an over-all scheme, and I am particularly interested in the section that outlines the fears the federal government had at that time that the provinces would hesitate to go along until they had a firm commitment in black and white that they were not going to be caught away out on a limb with expenditures which were far beyond the provincial resources. Then the federal government went on to point out the following:
A province's participation In the plan would begin
(1)	Upon a province making use of the proposed planning and organization grant within 18 months and presenting a plan, satisfactory to the governor in council, describing the existing services and benefits in the province and the stages by which benefits will be provided and the full health insurance plan put into effect:
(2)	within the same period of 18 months making an agreement with the federal government to provide the initial benefits for the first stage of general practitioner services, hospital care and visiting nursing services within two years of the signing of the agreement. The agreement should further provide for the carrying into effect of the total health insurance program over a term of years, for a registration fee to be paid by or on behalf of every person, who has attained his 16th birthday and whose normal place of residence is in the province or area where benefits are provided . . .

Then may I take advantage of your invitation and offer a few remarks on the subject of the amendment. My purpose is to submit to you that the amendment is in order.
This is a resolution preceding, of course, what is known as a money bill, and I recognize that the type of amendment which can be introduced at this stage of the proceedings must conform with certain well-known requirements. In my submission this amendment does conform with those well-established requirements for an amendment to a resolution contemplating the introduction of a money bill.
May I first observe, Mr. Chairman, precisely what is the effect of the amendment. The resolution which has been moved by the Minister of National Health and Welfare contemplates the introduction of a measure:
... to authorize contributions to be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund to provinces in respect of costs incurred by them and providing insured hospital and diagnostic services pursuant to provincial law and to agreements made in accordance with the said measure . . .
And the payments out of the consolidated revenue fund are to commence, according to the resolution, when at least six provinces, containing at least half the population of Canada, have entered into such agreements and qualified for the receipt of such contributions. The amendment does not touch the

opening clause of the resolution at all. That still remains in the present form:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize contributions to be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund . . .
And so on. The amendment deals only with the time at which, or the conditions under which, the payments may be inaugurated. Instead of the requirement that there be at least six provinces containing at least half the population of Canada having entered into agreements, the amendment would substitute the provision that the whole scheme should be inaugurated or commence when any province of Canada has entered into the agreement. There is an essential point there, Mr. Chairman. It is that the amendment does not touch the main body of the resolution; it simply relates to the date on which, or the circumstances under which, the scheme may commence.
The references I should like respectfully to offer to you, Mr. Chairman, commence at page 169 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition. The first is citation 440, which reads:
The fundamental terms of a money resolution submitted to the house with the Governor General's recommendation upon which a committee of the whole is set up cannot be amended. Amendments will only be in order if they fall within the terms of the resolution.
I emphasize these words, "if they fall within the terms of the resolution". It is my submission that this amendment is of a kind which does fall within the terms of the resolution now under debate. I conclude reading citation 440:
The procedure in committee on those resolutions follows in principle the procedure of the committee of supply, and amendments are out of order if they are proposed with a view to substituting an alternative scheme to that proposed with the royal recommendation.
I emphasize, sir, that the amendment in no sense offers an alternative scheme to that proposed in the royal recommendation. It accepts the royal recommendation; it accepts the scheme which is proposed; it simply concerns itself with the date on which and the circumstances under which that scheme can be brought into operation.
There are examples in citations 441 and 442 of amendments which have been ruled out of order because in effect they proposed alternative schemes to that proposed with the royal recommendation. For instance, in citation 442 there are amendments proposing to substitute a loan for a subsidy; to change the destination, purpose and conditions of a subsidy; attaching a condition to a subsidy; affecting the ends and provisions of a subsidy.

But, sir, may I next draw your attention to citation 444, which reads as follows:
Private members may introduce resolutions that do not directly involve the expenditure of public money and have no operative effect but simply express an abstract opinion on a matter which may necessitate a future grant.
Now, sir, there is a point that I think with respect has to be considered at this time. The resolution contemplates the introduction of a bill. It is quite clear that the bill in turn, in addition to what is contained in the resolution, would require the appropriation of money by parliament in the form of a supplementary appropriation if it were to be brought into effect during the fiscal year to commence April 1, 1957; or an estimate, if it is to be brought into effect in the following fiscal year, whatever it might be. And that, it seems to me, is no suggestion that the amendment would involve any increase in public expenditure.
It is quite correct that the amendment, by easing the conditions under which the hospital insurance scheme may be brought into effect, in that way may accelerate- indeed, it is intended to accelerate-the inauguration of the scheme, the effective date of it. It is quite true that is certainly the intention of the amendment, and it is the effect it would have. It still requires a later vote of supply.
In my submission the amendment is one falling within the terms of the resolution, according to the language of citation 440. It is not one that substitutes an alternative scheme to that proposed with the royal recommendation, according to the language used in citation 440, and it does not of itself create an increase in public expenditure. That would necessitate a supplementary appropriation.
For these reasons, sir, it is my submission that the amendment is in order and fully conforms with the recognized conditions to which an amendment to a money resolution must conform in this committee.

Mr. Chairman, it is not clear that the amendment, even as clarified, assists Your Honour in ruling in its favour. The clarification which, as I indicated a few moments ago, came to my attention, only a short time ago, has a restrictive effect, but that does not in any way change the character of the amendment.
The question before us is whether or not the amendment involves any kind of charge on the crown. The rule is pretty clear. My hon. friend who has just taken his seat has directed our attention to citations 440 and 441 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, but I am at a loss

to understand how he can seriously argue that these references help him in any way in this particular. Citation 440 is quite clear. It says:
The fundamental terms of a money resolution submitted to the house with the Governor General's recommendation upon which a committee of the whole is set up cannot be amended. Amendments will only be in order if they fall within the terms of the resolution. The procedure in committee on those resolutions follows in principle the procedure of the committee of supply, and amendments are out of order if they are proposed with a view to substituting an alternative scheme to that proposed with the royal recommendation.
The scheme proposed by the amendment is clearly an alternative one. It proposes that the federal government should pay money, not on the condition that there will be six provinces, as the resolution stipulates, but at the moment at which one province gives its acceptance. The federal government, according to the amendment, should on that account agree to pay moneys toward the realization of that particular scheme in that particular province, so that on the basis of citation 440 it is clearly out of order.
Citation 441 equally does not assist my hon. friend in his contention, and citation 437 is clearly on the point when it says:
No cases can be found of any private member in the Canadian commons receiving the authority of the crown, through a minister, to propose a motion involving the expenditure of public money. No principle is better understood than the constitutional obligation that rests upon the executive government, of alone initiating measures imposing charges upon the public exchequer.
That is precisely what this amendment does. The effect of the amendment, even as clarified, is to add to the financial burden on the crown, and it is therefore out of order.
The fact that it is suggested that the money required in a particular instance might be less seems at first glance to be attractive, but certainly it does not add to the strength of the argument, because the fact is that under the amendment as now proposed and clarified, expenditures would be involved in one province at a time when the crown does not intend to be so involved financially.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I have no great difficulty in supporting the ruling which you have indicated to be in your mind, holding this amendment to be one that is clearly not within the mischief of the rule as contemplated in this house.

Mr. Chairman, it is a
pleasure for me to take part in the debate on this resolution preceding legislation which has for its objective the alleviation of human misery and the sharing by society of some of the financial burden which from time to time may fall on individuals due to illness. That is not to say, of course, that I agree wholeheartedly with the proposed legislation in every particular, but I do think it is a step in the right direction though long overdue.
Seventy five years ago or so

in relatively recent times-medical attention from a financial point of view was a somewhat inexpensive matter compared to the expense it can involve today, because in those days when illness struck usually the only facilities available were the attention of a general practitioner and attention and convalescence in the home.
In that connection I might point out that many general practitioners performed great service for the poorer classes in our communities by being very generous in forgetting to send bills in cases where they knew it would be difficult for the people to pay. The work that has been done by the general practitioner over the years for the benefit of society in this regard cannot be overstated, and it is something for which we should all be grateful.

speechtext: Dr. W. J. P. MacMillan in Prince Edward Island is an excellent example.

Yes, a perfect example. In those days if the attention the general practitioner could provide and home treatment were not sufficient to provide a cure the case was generally considered hopeless, because no facilities existed anywhere else that could effect a cure. You were faced then with the reality that the case was probably hopeless.
Great advances have been made in medical science in the last 75 years, one of the most important being the invention of the X-ray. However, all these advances brought with them complications in the form of greater expense and the necessity of bringing the patient to a central point such as a hospital where these facilities would be available. Cures are obtained regularly today which 75 years ago would have been considered phenomenal if not almost beyond belief.
The use of these specialized forms of treatment brought with them added expenses as far as the individual was concerned and, as I have said already, the necessity of treatment in a hospital. As a result many individuals faced with illness today find that the cost involved may prove to be a catastrophe from
Health Insurance
the financial point of view. It is something the average family cannot afford, or if they do pay these costs it quite often leaves them in an economically unfavourable position for many years. A family might be faced with having to forgo the education of children and such things which should not have to be considered.
However, we live in a civilization which believes that human life is beyond price. In line with that philosophy we believe that cost in itself should not be a deterrent to restoring individuals to health if the means are available to do it. In addition to the necessity for hospitalization brought about by these new techniques, which involve added cost, there is the further increase in the general cost of hospitalization. As a result of all this the burden becomes almost impossible for the average family to pay, and as a result a prolonged sickness can prove to be a near catastrophe.
Some people may be lucky enough to gd through their lives without having to enter a hospital, but in this day and age we find that more and more people start their lives in a hospital and perhaps end them there as well, even though they may be lucky enough to not require hospitalization during the years between. But there are others who are not so fortunate. Although the burden of illness may be crushing for the individual, it should be something that could be borne by society at large. Therefore the sensible thing to do is to introduce the insurance principle so the load may be carried by society as a whole, and in that way prevent disaster coming to any family or individual because of sickness or accident.
I have said that the advances in medical science have brought about a general increase in the cost of treatment and hospitalization. However, it should not be forgotten that because of these advances in medical science great savings have been achieved in the way of time and money. The advances in preventive medicine have proved of great benefit to our society. Medical science has succeeded in eliminating a number of diseases which had disastrous consequences in the past, and I refer particularly to smallpox, diphtheria, and we hope polio as well. As a result of these advances in medical science it has been made easier for society to carry the remaining burden, and that is something that should not be forgotten.
There is still a great field open in this regard for the curing of disease, and any advance in that direction will be of great benefit. I believe money spent to that end will return dividends from an economic point

of view as well as in the form of the elimination of human suffering. There are still diseases for which there seems to be no cure, and my feeling is that research should be pressed in order to find some means of combating diseases such as multiple sclerosis and cancer. Early diagnosis can pay dividends economically as well as eliminate needless suffering.
It may be said by some that this business of finding cures for diseases which a few years ago would have been fatal in most cases runs counter to the principle of the survival of the fittest; that if we carry on long enough we will succeed in creating a race susceptible to every ill to which man is subject, and the incidence of disease will increase so the long-range result may prove that we have adopted a self-defeating program. Nevertheless we believe that human life is priceless, and that nothing should stand in the way, even momentarily, of achieving the ends we have in view at the present time.
In this connection I believe there is a great field for research into heredity, so we may have a wider knowledge of the results of heredity upon susceptibility to disease. That might result in a healthier population, which would decrease the incidence of sickness and the need for hospitalization.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I had already commented on the great services of general practitioners, especially in the past, to the people of the communities in which they laboured. I want to thank the minister in that connection for his recognition of the services that a distinguished resident of my province, Dr. W. J. P. MacMillan, has rendered to the community generally as far as all problems of health are concerned. Just at six o'clock I was pointing out that I considered that pressing on with medical research is an effort that can be highly justified from every point of view.
I now want to turn for a few moments to the application of the proposed legislation to the provinces. The minister pointed out that the formula which he proposes is weighted slightly in favour of the provinces that will find the burden most difficult to carry. I think it is commendable that the minister has even nodded in the direction of the need of such recognition, but I do not think the recognition goes far enough.

At the time of confederation the taxgathering capacity of the provinces and their responsibilities were fairly well balanced, but since confederation the tax fields over which the federal government has jurisdiction have proved to be the most lucrative ones, the ones which have expanded most over the years, while with the exception of defence and a few other fields of that sort, the greatest expansion of responsibility has been in the fields which are the responsibilities of the provinces. This legislation is an example of the sort of thing to which I refer. Social security of all types is another example.
As time goes by there is an ever-increasing discrepancy between the resources of the provinces and their obligations, and the various types of matching grants which the federal government has proposed to the provinces from time to time are not by any means the answer as far as the poorer provinces are concerned. Here we have a situation where the federal government in relation to the provinces is rather in the same position as a wealthy man coming along and offering to sell a bankrupt a Cadillac at half price. Something you cannot afford is not a bargain at any price. The person who is pretty nearly down and out would probably more appreciate a free pair of boots than a Cadillac at half price, because the latter is beyond his reach and is really no benefit at all.
The premier of my province, speaking in the legislature the other day with regard to this proposal, said it is definitely beyond the financial capabilities of the province of Prince Edward Island at the present time, and therefore out of reach of the people of that province. If that is the case, it can be of no benefit to them in the immediate future. When speaking in the legislature Premier Matheson had this to say:
There is a limit to the type of gift Ottawa gives through matching grants and that limit is the economic resources of the province.
It is estimated that the cost of this scheme to Prince Edward Island would be approximately $1,130,000 a year in addition to their present expenditures in this field. While that may sound like a small amount to the federal government, it is something my province cannot afford because over the last number of years the province of Prince Edward Island has been going into debt by about this amount annually.
I believe the other maritime provinces will also find it extremely difficult to take advantage of this legislation. I am afraid that from the point of view of the maritimes its principle is the old biblical one, namely, that to him that hath shall be given and from him that hath not even that which he hath shall be taken away.

In order that a proposal might be evolved which would be within the reach of the maritime provinces, I think consideration should be given to some special aspects of this proposal. The first is that the general share of the federal responsibility should be increased. I feel that the maritime provinces cannot possibly with any degree of ease take advantage of this proposal unless the federal share is at least 60 per cent.
Then there are other considerations which I would commend to the minister. In my opinion hospital depreciation, as has already been pointed out by several other members, should be considered one of the expenses in which the federal government will share.

Having said that I should like to point out that as far as the provinces are concerned, I feel that no real solution to the problem-and I recognize that this is not only the responsibility of the Minister of National Health and Welfare-will be arrived at until the whole field of dominion-provincial fiscal policy is readjusted.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to be able to say a few words in this debate on national health insurance. I hope we shall label it by its right name. It is a national hospital insurance plan and not a national health insurance plan such as we have looked forward to for many years.
Health Insurance
I hope this plan is not once again a hoax being perpetrated on the people of Canada in order to enable the Liberals to win yet another election. I think the people of Canada have had enough of the use of national health insurance as a political football in order to get the Liberal party into office, and then having it promptly forgotten once the election is over. The Canadian people have heard this story ever since 1919, as has already been pointed out. On one occasion the Liberals even had the audacity to present a bill to the House of Commons, or rather to table a bill and go to the people and mislead them into thinking that the bill would become an actuality if the Liberals were returned to power.
If this is not to be a repeat performance I would say the Liberal party could well show that this time it means what it says when it speaks of national health insurance, and that it could accept the challenge being issued by the spokesmen of the western provinces. The challenge is this. If you mean what you say, pay now to each of the provinces who are ready to take you up on your offer and to proceed. I think that would be a fair request for these people in the west to make of the Liberals at this election. If they are sincere, are they willing to amend the legislation they are now proposing to enable the government to pay now and not to pay as far away as 1960 if by then enough provinces agree to enter the scheme.
I come from British Columbia, the fastest growing province in Canada. I am extremely pleased to notice that the latest issue of the Financial Post, the issue of March 23, devotes a special section to outlining the tremendous developments that are taking place in our province at the west coast. However, such a rapid growth also brings with it a large number of problems. They are mainly social problems. We might very well have had attached to this newspaper another special circular outlining some of the unusually severe difficulties which we have in our province and which are partly caused by the rapid industrial expansion and the growth in our population.
One of the problems we have is directly related to the essence of the resolution before us. I refer to the problem of hospital construction costs. One of the municipalities in my riding-and I am referring now to Burnaby-in 1931 had some 30,000 people. In 1957 it has 83,000. The same story can be told for almost any of our industrial areas there. We are obliged to build new hospitals, new schools and other social needs almost more rapidly than our architects are able to design them.

Health Insurance
I greatly regret that the minister has indicated, if not today at least on other occasions, that the capital costs of hospitals cannot be included in the plan. Some years ago I pointed out to the minister that his grant of $1,000 per bed for the building of a new hospital is entirely unrealistic in the light of what has happened to the costs of building hospitals since the plan was first begun. To build additions to the Vancouver general hospital costs at the rate of $20,000 per bed. For the federal government to offer $1,000 out of $20,000 is leaving a very large share on the shoulders of the provincial and municipal governments and to the volunteer efforts of our good citizens. Even a moderate hospital cannot be built at the present time in British Columbia at less than $10,000 a bed.
The federal grant is only 10 per cent of the capital expense. I realize that all the rest of it-the $9,000 to $19,000 per bed-must be raised partly by voluntary effort, partly by a tax on real estate in municipalities, and in part by grants from the provincial government. The niggardly attitude of the federal government in this regard, especially as it applies to rapidly growing areas of Canada, is to be regretted.
I have yet to hear the government advance a sound argument or I have yet to hear them advance any argument-they may have done so but I am unaware of it-as to why they cannot include capital costs in this program. I should also like to know why they cannot include the costs of administration. The government will find that this problem of capital costs of hospitalization is going to be more severe than ever once their plan gets under way; because in Saskatchewan, in British Columbia and in Great Britain experience has shown that once you introduce a hospital plan for all, your hospitals immediately become greatly overloaded at least for the first several years of such a plan.
With regard to the problem that will be faced I should like to read into the record what was said by the premier of British Columbia in his budget speech of 1954. This will be found at page 18:
The most difficult, most pressing, and certainly the most vexing problem requiring early and realistic solution is the provision of comprehensive hospital insurance at a reasonable and equitable cost to all of our people.
A few years from now I can picture the Minister of National Health and Welfare, not the one who is now occupying that post but some other person, rising in his place and having to admit to the parliament of Canada that this business of hospital insurance is certainly a complex problem.
I was pleased to hear the minister make some reference to the fact that the plan [Mr. Hegler.l
envisaged taking care of chronic cases. I hope we will hear a little more of the details in that regard when the bill is introduced. We in British Columbia look with some envy at Saskatchewan where, as long as the doctor certifies you as being in need of hospital care, you can obtain hospital care without any fee whatever. This is not so in our province. We are anxiously looking forward to the day when, either through the help of the federal government or through our own government in British Columbia, we will have hospital care without charge for our chronically ill people.
I regret that mental cases in mental institutions are not going to be included. In my riding there is a mental institution at Esson-dale in which there are upwards of 5,000 mentally ill people. I see no reason why there should be this discrimination against them. This government gets over 70 per cent of every tax dollar; and simply because most of the provincial governments have now assumed full responsibility for mental care as well as for T.B. care the federal government saw a way of saving some money. I think this is ducking the responsibility simply because another government, in former years, has seen fit to assume that responsibility. This is no reason why the care of these people should now be excluded from the plan.
I should like to spend just a minute or two on the vast amount of propaganda we have been fed over the past several years warning the Canadian people that health insurance would ruin the economy of Canada. I should like to ask those people who have been carrying on this propaganda just who pays now for the health care of our people. Most of our people have to pay their own bills. Hundreds of millions of dollars are being paid by the people of Canada when they pay their doctor bills, hospital bills and dental bills, so there is this tremendous sacrifice by the people in terms of dollars and cents.
In many cases health care is being paid for by people who have to mortgage their homes in order to meet unusually heavy medical bills. Boys and girls of 15, 16 and 17 are having to leave high school because of illness in the family and the economic hardship involved. This is a loss to our nation, when young boys and girls are forced to leave school without finishing their education. This lack of health care is being paid for, in many cases, with the lives of our people.
I am sure all of us in this house know of individuals who, had they received adequate health care as it could have been supplied under a national health program, would have been alive today and useful citizens.

We suffer a great deal of economic loss by way of unemployment caused by the illness of Canadian working people. The deficits of the hospitals from one end of Canada to the other are being paid for, in some cases by religious organizations but in most cases by municipalities. These losses represent a burden on the home owners. Health care is being paid for also by the sacrifices made by those who work in our hospitals from one end of Canada to the other. I feel the day is long past when our nurses-in-training should have to obtain money from outside sources in order to keep themselves in the institutions where they are working toward their nursing degree. These nurses have made tremendous sacrifices over the years to maintain the standards of efficiency of our hospitals. The other help in most hospitals of Canada are being greatly underpaid. It is time these wage earners had their wages brought into line with the general level of wages paid in Canada.
We as a nation, in one way or another, pay for our health care now in a haphazard manner which is uneconomical, and a lot of people who need it most have to do without it. The nation as a whole, under a national hospital scheme, would be much better off than under the present scheme. We in the C.C.F. movement believe it is up to the strong to help the weak. We believe, as the hon. member for Queens pointed out, that at some time or other all of us have used or will use hospitals. We believe that when we are well is the time for working men to pay for the days when they are going to be ill.
I ask the government, before appealing to the country for support on its national hospital scheme, to promise to pay now to the provinces that are ready to proceed. I do not think the minister meant exactly what he said the other day. At page 2612 of Hansard for Friday, March 22, 1957 the minister said:
-the federal government made a proposal to the provinces under which we are undertaking to provide 50 per cent of the public ward hospital costs of every individual in every consenting province.
I believe he rectified that in the statement he made this afternoon. The statement he made on Friday should have been amplified by saying that if the governments of the provinces will agree to the scheme, then beginning January 1, 1959, we will assume some responsibility. We are asking, when do we get some of this money? We are very much concerned. According to the statement filed by the premier of British Columbia on February 22 last, when he presented the 1957-58 budget, the net estimated outlay for hospital services was $33,666,800. According to the statement by the Minister of
Health Insurance
National Health and Welfare we would have received a grant of at least $16 million a year toward that. This $16 million a year is a lot of money to be losing. I understand that if the plan goes through as announced our first payment will be received in 1960, for 1959. In other words, for the years 1957 and 1958 we are to receive nothing, so we lose $32 million.
If this government is sincere in offering hospital insurance to the people of Canada this year, then we in British Columbia have the right to demand a payment of $16 million this year and $16 million next year.
We hate to lose that $32 million, which we feel is ours. If this parliament passes a law establishing a principle, then those areas of Canada which live up to the principle should be entitled to their fair share of the amount available. In fact the people of Saskatchewan and the people of British Columbia should not be discriminated against. If anything they should be given some extra consideration, because the many experiences those two provinces have gone through are going to be of great value to not only the federal government but to other provinces as well that are attempting to introduce hospital schemes. We feel that we are being robbed of $32 million; and if this government means what it says, and if this is not just an election hoax, it will agree to pay us that $32 million over the next two years.
The interesting feature of this whole national health insurance program, Mr. Chairman, is the attitude shown by the various political movements in our country. In the province of Saskatchewan there are many areas known as health regions where people are supplied with medical, dental and hospital care without any special fee at the time those services are used. Saskatchewan, under a C.C.F. government, was the first to establish a provincial hospital insurance plan. I wish the resolution introduced by the minister went further along this line. I am reading from "Share Canada's Wealth! The National C.C.F. Program". Under "Comprehensive Health Services" it has this to say:
A nation-wide health insurance plan to provide every man, woman and child in Canada with full medical, hospital, nursing, dental, optical and other health care, with the federal government paying 80 per cent of the cost and the provinces the remaining 20 per cent;
Decentralized administration in co-operation with the provincial governments, and with full freedom for everyone to choose his own family doctor.
I am very pleased to say that in British Columbia the Social Credit party, in my opinion at least, have undergone a very radical change in their attitude toward this whole problem. I can well recall how in

Health Insurance
1952 they went through the province and fought against our compulsory hospital scheme. They would remove the compulsory features from it. In fact in his budget speech in 1954 the premier of the province admitted that an "effort was made to convert the plan from a compulsory to a voluntary one".
Well, I suppose that was good politics at the time. However, I am sure that even at that time the premier of British Columbia knew that you could not successfully operate a hospital scheme if you were to allow to participate, or have in it, only the aged and the sick people, and let the healthy ones get away without entering the scheme. They have certainly undergone a change of heart. I hope they will have a further advance in that direction and will do something to expand and make a little more liberal the hospital insurance scheme that we now have.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: If it needs doing we will do it.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
It may well be that when they get the money from the federal government that is their due they will make some moves in that direction. If the hon. member for New Westminster had not been so hasty in interrupting he would have found that I was going to compliment the premier of my province on his last statement. At page 39 of his budget speech this year he had this to say:
The welfare of our people demands the earliest possible provision of a national health program embracing hospital, diagnostic, medical, surgical and dental care; it requires also that more generous and dental care; it requires also that more generous the government of Canada. The government of this province vigorously will press for action on both these matters.
I know interruptions are sometimes pretty good politics, but I do think members of the C.C.F. should be allowed to compliment a Social Credit premier when he finally realizes that health is a vital problem of the people, and that it deserves the recognition he has given it in his recent budget speech.
When we look at the attitude of the Progressive Conservative party I am pleased that the Minister of National Health and Welfare was able to outmanoeuvre the frosty Frost plan of the province of Ontario. I am convinced, and have been for months, that there was a sincere desire to use Ontario's hospital insurance plan as a political football in the province of Ontario in the forthcoming election. I think this has now been avoided. As I first saw the frosty Frost plan, it consisted of a sort of half-baked voluntary plan, with ample provision to allow all the

shyster health societies to keep on making a good rake-off at the expense of the poor people of the province.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: You are terribly wrong, and you know it.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
Companies selling their plans and taking up to 40 per cent in cost of overhead will now be eliminated. Of course the worst attitude of all was taken by the Liberal government of Manitoba. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre called it a disastrous plan. It was that, indeed. The very idea of offering to supply people with hospital coverage after they have been in hospital for six months. By that time I imagine the people would no longer be very interested in who would be paying the bills.
I spoke of the attitude of the Liberal government of the province of Manitoba, which again brings me back to the subject of just how sincere is the Liberal government that we have sitting across the way and now proposing a national hospital insurance plan. This house opened two and a half months ago. The session is about over; yet the minister waited until March 4 before he put his resolution on the order paper. When the resolution was put on the order paper and we thought now we were getting somewhere, the government saw fit to wait until March 25; three full weeks went by before we were given a chance to act on this resolution. It is rather odd that on the very day we are given our first chance at this resolution there also appears on the order paper a proposed motion indicating very clearly to us that our days in this house are numbered. Therefore we may not see the actual implementation of this hospital insurance plan.
I want to deal for just a moment with the sharing of the cost. I believe indications have been given that we in the province of British Columbia can expect to get somewhere around 45 per cent of our present hospital insurance plan paid for by the federal government. I believe we are under the 50 per cent. At any rate I think we receive the lowest of the percentages. I think most of us who have been following this subject for some years have always hoped that something in the neighbourhood of 70 per cent of the cost would be forthcoming from the federal treasury. Later, because of the statements made by Liberal spokesmen, we had to revise our figures downward and we finally came down to 60 per cent. Even the premier of British Columbia understood for a while that we could expect 60 per cent to come out of federal funds.
However, when I look for possible reasons why this government with its huge budget

surplus is offering the provinces only an average of 50 per cent, I think I am able to pinpoint the reason. I remember hearing this proposal as given in this very chamber on October 3, 1955, in the proceedings of the federal-provincial conference, when the premier of British Columbia-being perhaps too eager and not as shrewd a bargainer in this respect as he sometimes is-as reported at page 73 of the report said:
I can't help noting here, Mr. Prime Minister, that in the original submission by the national government, the federal offered to participate on a 60 per cent basis. Our province, being always fair, says we will now enter into a program on a 50 per cent basis with the national government.
I may say that during the recess that followed this statement I had occasion to speak to a few of the representatives of some of the other provincial governments, and they were all most annoyed at the premier of British Columbia coming out and offering to have his province pay 50 per cent of the cost. When a province offers to pay 50 per cent of the cost you can hardly blame the federal government for not offering to pay more in turn. After all, they would be accused of throwing money away needlessly if they did.
I come now to the last point I wish to make. I regret that the understanding that has been reached between the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the various ministers of health and premiers of the provinces has not helped the people of Canada in one respect. I realize there was nothing the minister could do about it, but what we in British Columbia would like to know is this. What is the provincial government going to do with the $16 million a year when and if they get it?
We in the C.C.F. party sincerely hope that when and if the federal government will be paying 45 per cent of the cost of our British Columbia hospital plan the new arrangement will also have some real significance for the people of that province by way of added health services. Although I am not going to deal with them now, there are many ways in which an additional $16 million could be well spent in my province in a further move toward the goal of a national health service, as the premier himself so ably outlined in his budget speech this session.

Health Insurance
been expecting and hoping for a measure of this kind for quite a number of years.
While we in the Conservative party welcome this resolution we regret that it has taken the present government and preceding governments 38 years to get around to the point of introducing it. Just to refute what the last speaker had to say I would point out that if it had not been for the action taken by Premier Frost of Ontario we might very well have had to wait another five years before this measure was introduced.
