maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
The Canadian people are well aware of the need for some measure of this kind. The very fact that 70 per cent of the Canadian people are now covered by some type of insurance indicates the extent to which they are interested in this subject, and demonstrates the hope that a co-ordinated scheme with the provinces might in some cases reduce the cost.
I do not think anyone should labour under the impression that this is going to be free. Someone is going to pay for it, and who could that be but the taxpayers of the country? The increasing cost of illness makes this measure imperative. I was very much interested in what was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Lanark who, in dealing with the subject of the increasing cost of illness, said that whereas the average patient per day cost in 1947 was $7.46, it had risen to $14.64 in 1954. I was speaking to the hospital authorities in my home city just last week, and I was informed that the per patient per day cost was something over $15 in that particular hospital last year.
We are glad that some form of universal coverage will be provided. I am inclined to doubt the wisdom of the statement made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who said that the greater part of the cost should be borne under a plan that would take it from those with the greatest ability to pay. He mentioned the corporations and large companies. What happens in a case like that is that their contribution becomes a part of the operating cost of the company, which will be added to the cost of the goods they sell and the consumer will be the person who pays ultimately, not the corporation. I do not think that plan is practical, and probably it is not as fair as many other schemes which could be proposed.
Many middle class people are fearful of rising hospitalization and medical costs, which in some cases are ruinous. I am going to cite

Health Insurance
two or three illustrations. These cases were brought to my attention just last week end when I was home. In one case a child was in hospital for seven days, and the Middlesex county co-operative medical services were carrying the risk. They paid the cost of hospitalization up to $7 per day. The cost of the room per day was $7.50 so in this case the family was charged only a total of $3.50 for the room. The unfortunate part of the case was that because of the rather peculiar type of illness the diagnostic and special examinations, including X-rays and tests of one kind and another, amounted to $154, or $22 a day for the period of seven days during which the child was confined to hospital. Although the family believed they were covered with insurance, they learned that their total costs were $157.50. That same family last year also had other medical expenses amounting to approximately $500. This is one case of which I had personal knowledge.
I was inquiring about some other cases, and learned of one near my home. The child involved was confined to hospital in St. Thomas. The parents, who were young farmers, received a bill amounting to $2,200. They had to put a second mortgage on their farm, and only after many years were they able to pay the bill.
I know of a similar case in which the breadwinner of the family, a working man, was stricken and the costs of his hospitalization and treatment amounted to $2,400. Following his recovery the man and many of the men who worked in the plant with him sold their blood in order to help eliminate the debt against him. This serves to point up how necessary it is to have some scheme of this kind.
It is well known, of course, that those in the higher income brackets can afford hospitalization and medical care and those in the townships and municipalities are taken care of, but the vast majority of middle class people find this an extremely difficult situation to meet.
We come now to another problem having to do with nurses and nurses in training. There is no doubt that with the inauguration of a plan of this kind there is an increased demand for hospitalization. I am told that the experience in other countries and other provinces has been similar to what we found with the introduction of television, when the attendance at theatres dropped off; and that is that with the inauguration of such a plan there is a high demand at the beginning, which levels off as time goes on. We know there is a shortage of nurses at the present time. A girl getting her matriculation may

enter hospital for training or she could enter teachers' college, where upon graduation she might earn anywhere up to $3,400. It might be pointed out that the supervisor of nurses at a hospital will receive about $3,500. There are probably not enough of our young ladies being attracted to the nursing profession.
Another matter to be considered is that not all hospitals have the same standing. I am thinking now of London, where we have a medical school whose students may attend the hospital to receive valuable experience and training for their medical careers. Some hospitals provide nursing training and others do not. These are some of the details with which no doubt the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the ministers of health in the various provinces will find it necessary to deal.
I would cite the case of a man in Ontario becoming seriously ill and being sent to the Montreal neurological institute. Until such time as Quebec enters the scheme the question would probably arise whether he would be eligible under this plan. That is something else that will have to be worked out. There is no doubt that the same coverage will be extended to all hospitals regardless of the type of training they may provide.
Some mention was made in the newspapers about the possibility of one or more of the existing health plans in the province being made the administrative core once the act came into force. I think I read something in the paper to the effect that some of the officials of the Blue Cross might provide this administrative core. I wonder about the advisability of that, because there are many other worth-while groups, and I am thinking particularly of P.S.I. and Associated Medical Services. Then I might mention that we have in Middlesex county the Middlesex co-operative medical services which provides health insurance at cost. I have looked into that plan and I find it is most comprehensive, being provided at a much more reasonable figure than that of the Blue Cross. No one organization has a corner on good ideas or on administration.
Perhaps I should not mention the Blue Cross in that way, because it has been said that they operate on 5 per cent of their income. I heard someone mention a 40 per cent cost, so I do not want anyone to get the impression I am against the Blue Cross because of their cost of administration, since I realize that a 5 per cent cost is fairly moderate.
There is another thing which we as Canadians should not overlook, and that is that in practically every province or nation where a health measure has been introduced it has

been found necessary to increase the rates. This is understandable, because we know that we learn by experience and rising costs due to the inflation that has been going on all over must be considered. We hope we will be able to level off, but if the inflation envisaged by the Gordon report continues we can look forward to ever-rising costs all down the line.
I do not wish to speak further, as there have been many hon. members, including the hon. member for Lanark, who have spoken on behalf of this party. But I do want to say that I think the vast majority of Canadians have been expecting and hoping for a plan of this kind for a long time, and we hope the minister will get on with the legislation.

Mr. Chairman, I feel I must say something on this resolution. I understand it was back in 1919 that the Liberal party first campaigned on the basis of a sickness insurance plan for Canada, now known as health insurance. Back in 1919 I was a student in public school, and since that time I have had a number of years in public life. In the federal House of Commons and in provincial legislatures we have had the representatives of different parties speaking in favour of health and hospital insurance. From a start in their campaign in 1919 we find the Liberals introducing a resolution on March 25, 1957. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has now presented a resolution covering hospital insurance.
There are occasions when perhaps we as members of parliament forget the work of those who are not members. I can remember my first session of the British Columbia legislature, in 1936. At that time there was a Liberal government and the minister of health and welfare, Hon. George Weir, introduced an over-all health insurance plan in February of that year.

Although the health insurance plan had been adopted by an act of the legislature the legislation was killed by the
Health Insurance
medical profession, who told Hon. George Weir that they would go on strike if he ever put it into effect. They not only killed the bill, but in my humble estimation they also killed Hon. George Weir.
However, the point I want to make at this time in speaking on the resolution is that although there have been parties in favour of such a plan and even legislation passed, there were also those who worked for a complete over-all health insurance program before the bill was introduced in the legislature of British Columbia. I refer to one man who worked for it and who became the first member of the board although the legislation never went into effect. He later came to Ottawa, and I believe he was employed for some time in the department of the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Because upon occasions such as this not enough tribute is paid to pioneers not known to the general public, on this day when we are debating the resolution preceding the introduction of the first bill that will provide a national health insurance plan I should like to pay my respects to Dr. Allon Peebles. Starting in 1932 he began the work which preceded the introduction of the bill in the legislature of British Columbia providing for a complete health insurance plan. He was the first commissioner appointed, and he worked for some time in Ottawa in the Department of National Health and Welfare. Though now and for a number of years very ill, he is still a resident of the city of Ottawa. On an occasion like this I believe that we should honour those who work behind the scenes. I am very sorry that neither the province of British Columbia nor the federal government of Canada has seen fit to assist this man in his illness.
A lot has been said by those who have preceded me about varying aspects of the resolution and why it is unfair that the provinces that have pioneered should be crucified and penalized until the others come under the plan. I am not going to speak on that aspect now, because all that could be said has already been said. What I want to do is draw the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare to a speech I made in the house about ten months ago. On that occasion I said that before there was a general election the government would introduce a hospital insurance bill, if not a health insurance bill. I was right. At that time I told the minister that a great many hospital beds would be required, and that whatever plan he introduced and irrespective of the formula, basically the federal government would be assuming approximately 50 per cent of the cost of hospitalization.

Health Insurance
I pointed out then, and I do so again, that as the federal government will not start to pay for at least two years after the passage of the legislation, now is the time to spend money in order to save money. I refer naturally to the federal government's contributions to the construction of hospitals for chronic and convalescent cases. I am not referring to chronic cases from the point of view of what are generally recognized as chronic cases in the medical sense. I am referring to convalescents who now have to remain in hospitals for acute cases.
I do not want to repeat to any great extent what I said last year, but in view of the fact that apparenty it did not sink in, since no action has been taken, I think I should at least give the broad general principles. In the vast majority of cases it is not necessary for people having entered a hospital for acute cases and having received treatment to remain in such a hospital. They can easily be moved to a hospital for convalescents if it is adjacent. I am told by hospital authorities and doctors that the cost of caring for a person convalescing from an acute illness is approximately half the cost of caring for that person if he remains in a hospital for acute cases. I am told by the minister's own department that the cost of building a wing for convalescents on a hospital for acute cases is between 50 per cent and 60 per cent of the cost of building an acute hospital.
As I understand the resolution now before us, and work out the formula any way you want, it actually means in the broad analysis a payment of approximately 50 per cent of the cost of hospitalization. That being so, and inasmuch as the minister is going to have to spend the taxpayers' money, the minister is interested not only in giving proper treatment and care but in doing so at the lowest possible cost.
Under these circumstances I should like to make this appeal to the minister. Under other legislation he now pays $1,000 a bed in the construction of hospitals for acute cases and $1,500 a bed in the construction of hospitals for convalescent or chronic cases. I suggest to the minister that by way of aid and encouragement to the provinces that may come under the legislation envisaged by the resolution, and in the interests of giving proper treatment and care at the lowest possible cost, the minister should increase the amount for the construction of hospitals for convalescents adjacent to hospitals for acute cases.
I am absolutely convinced-and I have seen no arguments whatsoever in any way, shape or form to show me that I am wrong-that the

expenditure of money on convalescent hospitals adjacent to hospitals for acute cases will in the long run mean a great saving to those who are obliged to pay the taxes, and also a more efficient operation of hospitalization itself.
Along the same line may I suggest through you, Mr. Chairman, to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that he give more than lip service to the usage of naturopathy and physiotherapy. I am speaking now on the resolution under which the federal government is going to pay half the cost of hospitalization. The concern of the minister, I am sure, is not the money, though he must be concerned in part with that aspect; but in the main his concern is for the health of the people of Canada. I am convinced that we in Canada are missing the boat. We still insist upon being ruled by orthodox medicine, and we have refused so far to take advantage of the knowledge of the world of naturopathy and physiotherapy. It is being done in part in the hospitals today. It could be greatly extended.
I repeat what I have said I believe on three occasions in this house. Canada can eventually be known as the health mecca of the world. The minister was kind enough to refer this matter to his own research department and to make application to the C. R. Best institute to see if they could undertake some studies in that direction.
But because of this resolution and what it means, not just in the interests of the taxpayers but in the interests of the health of the people, I should like to ask if in your hospitalization regulations and details more thought and attention cannot be given to naturopathy and physiotherapy.
After this resolution passes, followed by the bill, when the scheme goes into effect in 1958 or 1959 the cost of hospitalization will be of quite great concern to the minister and his department. I am not going to repeat what has been said by others. I just want to add my words to those that have been spoken, and to pay my tribute to a man not very much known prior to 1935; I refer to Dr. Allon Peebles.
I want to ask that the minister give some thought to this matter now, in the two years before this plan goes into effect. I understand it will take about two years to do so. Perhaps by spending money now on convalescent hospitals adjacent to hospitals for acute cases and by the use of nature's own work and those who know it, it may mean a great deal in the administration of this new principle, a saving of money and a granting of new health to the people of this country.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure all members of this group are greatly pleased

that the resolution has been introduced. We naturally welcome any step forward toward an over-all health program. Our only regret is that this legislation has been delayed for so many years, and that it is not a great deal more comprehensive than is indicated by the resolution.
I was elected to this house in 1945, and I can remember that at that time and for a few years thereafter, the main discussion with regard to health matters was with respect to the government's proposal to the provinces contained in the now famous green books. The government's proposals at that time were much more comprehensive than anything contained in this resolution. At that time the government looked forward to an over-all program of health insurance in which the federal government would pay approximately 60 per cent of the cost of major health services.
We have waited 12 years since that time, and instead of the government today making to any province that will come in an offer to pay part of the cost of an over-all health insurance program, we have a resolution that covers a hospitalization program only; and as I understand the minister's statement, no payments will be made to any province, even though that province has a hospitalization plan at present in effect, until six provinces are prepared to inaugurate a hospitalization program and in fact are in a position to receive money for a program that is in operation or is about to commence operation.
I hope I am mistaken. If I am, I should certainly not be speaking at this time. As I understand it, in practical terms the statement is that the province of Saskatchewan-and the province of British Columbia, I take it, as well-will be obliged to wait in all probability until January 1, 1959, before any moneys are paid by the federal government under the terms of the present resolution.
The people of Saskatchewan have already been waiting for many years with a hospitalization program already in operation. The province of Saskatchewan led the way in Canada by implementing the first scheme of over-all hospitalization insurance. It has been most successful over the years. Although it was opposed at the time by members of the opposition in the Saskatchewan legislature, it is now, as far as principle is concerned, a program that is above and beyond political discussion, because no political party in the province of Saskatchewan would dare to oppose the Saskatchewan hospitalization program.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare this afternoon said that one particular provision of the bill would relate to the
Health Insurance
amount of deterrent charge or co-insurance that might be levied. I am proud that in Saskatchewan we have no deterrent charge, and that anybody whose doctor says he should be hospitalized is able to go to the hospital and obtain hospital care as provided by the plan without a deterrent charge or without coinsurance.
That is one of the features of the Saskatchewan plan which I believe is most important, and which puts it well to the fore with respect to all hospitalization plans in Canada.
I think sometimes we are inclined to think that a health program has as its chief or perhaps its whole purpose merely the paying of the cost of hospitalization or the cost of health services when they may be required. This is important. It is important to remove the financial burden from those who are sick, or from their dependents, or from the breadwinner. However, just as important are the added facilities and the better services that can be made available by a hospitalization program operated by a province, or a health program that might be assisted by a national plan.
I have had people close to the Saskatchewan hospitalization plan tell me that in Saskatchewan services are provided in hospitals that are not available in hospitals of comparable size in Manitoba or Alberta. They tell me that facilities in Saskatchewan are available in hospitals of a given size that are not available in other provinces.
This afternoon the Minister of National Health and Welfare mentioned the contributions the federal government had made through hospital construction grants. Then he mentioned that other grants were made available by the provinces. He did not mention, and I do not think he overlooked this intentionally, the very important role played by local governments, by municipal hospital districts and by religious orders. It is true that the largest amount of money has come by way of grants from provincial and federal governments, but the initiative in the building of hospitals has come from the local people and the local governments themselves.
One advantage of the Saskatchewan hospitalization plan is that a local district which is embarking upon the construction of a hospital can build and equip it with the full knowledge that the cost of the building, the cost of the equipment which is amortized over the life of the building or the equipment, will be paid for by the grants to which the minister referred and by the payments under the Saskatchewan hospitalization plan. The fact that the financial burden of building and equiping hospitals is removed from

Health Insurance
the backs of municipalities in local districts enables us to provide a standard of hospital service and a standard of equipment that, I suggest, cannot be matched in any other province under any local or privately operated scheme.
I could go on to point out that the Saskatchewan provincial scheme does not control the operation of the local hospitals. The hospitals are autonomous. Their operations are governed by the local boards. The hospitalization plan merely says to them, depending on the standard of service you provide we shall pay you the average cost of providing those services. There is no control at the provincial level over the operation of the hospitals.
I had hoped the Minister of National Health and Welfare could announce that a grant would be made by the federal government under this legislation to cover hospitalization of patients in provincial mental institutions, as well as for the hospitalization of patients in provincial sanitoria. Until these patients are covered the scheme will not be adequate and will not be comprehensive.
In recent years the Saskatchewan hospitalization plan has been costing something in excess of $22 million annually. I believe that in 1955 the figure was just over $22 million. I am informed, though I cannot say whether these figures are accurate-the minister, I think, would know-that under the government's proposed legislation this province would have a claim, on the basis of the 1955 operations of the Saskatchewan hospitalization service, to approximately $10 million from the federal treasury.
It is because Saskatchewan needs this additional money, because Saskatchewan wants to extend its health service, that we are so concerned about the provision which, as I understood the minister this afternoon, gives each of the first six provinces going into the plan the power to veto payments to the other five. Under the plan, as I understood the minister to outline it this afternoon, Saskatchewan will get nothing in 1957 and will receive no payment in 1958. Saskatchewan will have to wait until January 1, 1959, as the earliest possible date, under the minister's conditions, before receiving any money.
The people of Saskatchewan have now been waiting since their plan began operations more than 10 years ago. They are tired of waiting. They believe the federal government should have gone a lot further than it did in implementing its own proposals of 1945, its green book proposals. The government has retracted the health insurance program and retrenched until it is offering just

a hospitalization program, so it should not provide the further impediment that no payments will be made from the national treasury under this scheme until six provinces have plans in operation.
Saskatchewan is proud of the plan it now has. I have had no consultation whatever with any member of the Saskatchewan government as to what the Saskatchewan government might do if this program were to be made effective immediately. Hon. members will realize that the Saskatchewan government could do one of two things. It could reduce its own costs under the hospitalization tax or, alternatively, it could expand its health program. I do not know what the government might do, but I imagine it might do both those things.
The people of Saskatchewan want an extension of the health program. They have extended it in certain regions now to cover all medical expenses. The people of Saskatchewan led all Canada in the hospitalization program brought in 10 years ago. I have no doubt that the people of Saskatchewan stand ready today to be the first in experimenting in further extensions of the present health program. They do feel that the minister and the government are being shortsighted, are being small minded, in fact are discriminating against the province which went ahead in good faith 10 years ago in the light of the government's proposals at that time.
I can say this to the minister. The people of Saskatchewan will be critical of any legislation that forces them to wait another two years until the federal government becomes a full partner in the hospitalization program. The important thing is not that Saskatchewan is asking for money. It is that a hospitalization program in Saskatchewan and in any other province will provide more adequate health and hospital services for the people in those provinces. One has only to walk into some of the hospital institutions to realize how badly they are in need of money. I can believe that in the rich province of Ontario a great many hospitals would welcome such a hospital program, not only because it would improve the services to the people coming into those institutions, but it would in fact enrich the treasuries of the hospitals themselves so they could provide a better standard of service.
The people of Saskatchewan are asking the minister and the government to take another look at the statement made by the Prime Minister in January, a year ago, and the statement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare today. Take another look at it, and give Saskatchewan the green

light to show Canada how we can pioneer in an extension of health services.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I propose to take but a few moments in closing the debate to express to the committee the satisfaction one naturally must have in finding this measure so widely supported in all sections of the house. It is true that some hon. members have suggested additional features, but I think a review of all the statements that have been made will show that this resolution commends itself to all sections of the house, as I am sure it will to all sections of the country.
Much has been said about one or two points, and because I understand that there is a disposition now, in view of the importance of the matter, not to discuss the bill on second reading tomorrow, rather than have some misinterpretations go out I think possibly I might as well deal with them at this moment.
Reference has been made to tuberculosis control and mental illness not being regarded as insurable illnesses except for those suffering from these diseases in general hospitals. I think the situation will be generally understood when I point out that in those provinces in Canada, where they now have hospital insurance schemes, such as the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, they do not themselves include tuberculosis or mental diseases as insurable diseases. In the case of Saskatchewan they are covered in a separate account, but are not provided for in the premium system they have for the hospital insurance scheme in that province.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: They are covered.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: And they are free.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: That is the fact. They are not covered under the hospital insurance scheme. The same is true in British Columbia and in Alberta.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: They are free in Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
Yes, but it is not part of the hospital insurance scheme. Tuberculosis and mental illness are provided for almost to the extent of 90 per cent of the cost in most provinces out of the consolidated funds of the provinces themselves. That was revealed to us at the conference we had with all the ministers of health and the provincial treasurers a year ago. Likewise, in all countries I know of but one, tuberculosis and mental illnesses are not treated as insurable diseases.
That does not mean to say, as the interjections have properly noted, that the responsible governments do not look after the tubercular
Health Insurance
and those who are mentally ill. Of course they do, and of course they should and must, and they will continue to do so in this country. But it would be wrong by any principle, in addition to what I have revealed to be the situation, for us to include as part of the hospital insurance scheme tuberculosis patients and mentally ill people who receive treatment in provincial institutions.
Those individuals in Canada who will pay for their mental illness treatment and their tuberculosis treatment in general hospitals will be insurable under the scheme that is now covered by the resolution before the committee. In addition to that, under the national health program we will continue, as we have done in the past, to enable the provinces to carry on their important work of treatment and research in the fields of tuberculosis and mental illnesses. Therefore the impression should not go out into the country that there is no interest in those unfortunate individuals who suffer from mental illnesses or tuberculosis; that they are being ignored by this scheme. They are not being ignored in Canada; they are simply not being covered in this particular measure, except in the case of those in general hospitals, for the simple reason that they are now being taken care of substantially by the provinces, who regard them as their normal charges.
What we are seeking to do in this measure is to provide assistance to individual Canadian citizens to help them to bear their hospital costs. By this measure we are not seeking to subsidize the provinces in respect of responsibilities which they have normally regarded, and continue to regard, as their own.

The result is that the maritime provinces will receive greater percentages of contributions as a result of this formula from the federal government. The federal government will not in any way interfere with the way in which the provinces will raise their share of the money; in fact it would have no legal authority to do so. That would be the responsibility of the provincial governments, just as it would be our responsibility to find ways and means of raising our share which in the first year of operation, assuming 10 participating provinces, will come close to $200 million.
The provinces will have this advantage. At the present time in all provinces, in varying amounts and proportions, individuals subscribe to such hospital insurance schemes as the Blue Cross, some co-operative agricultural hospital insurance schemes, and other contractual arrangements with commercial companies and so on, so that a considerable percentage of the population in every province is now habituated in some way toward paying premiums for hospital costs. They will continue to pay premiums in the case of consenting provinces to provincially-sponsored schemes, so that taking into account the number of people who have been paying these premiums the net economic load of each province will certainly be much lighter than that borne by the federal government, not in respect of one particular jurisdiction but in respect of the whole country, or at any rate in respect of all the provinces which will agree to participate.
When hon. gentlemen argue that the federal government should assume responsibility for capital debt, depreciation and so on, as was suggested, what they are asking is that the federal government should assume a much greater burden than it is assuming under present arrangement which is much

more generous-four of five times, if one will analyse it-than the proposal of 1945.
No one in this house should think for a moment that in adopting this resolution we are proposing something that represents an inadequate contribution on the part of the federal government. As the treasurer of the province of Saskatchewan himself said at the conference, and so did the minister of health of British Columbia-and I thank them for the observation-the figures I have recited tonight indicate that the financial proposal made by the federal government is indeed a very generous one that will go a long way toward meeting the burden of individual hospital care in this country.
I want to make it perfectly clear that notwithstanding the provocations, if I may put it that way, or the temptations, I am not going to seek to try and suggest in this debate that this particular province or that particular political personality in a province has held up this scheme or is responsible for it. The facts are clear: the proposal was made by the Prime Minister of Canada following eight years of careful preparation on a co-operative basis with the provinces. In my judgment all the provinces have been seriously considering this matter, looking at it in the light of their responsibilities, and I say that the provinces without exception have taken a responsible attitude toward this problem.
If we establish a hospital insurance scheme, as we are obviously now going to, it will not be because of the efforts of one particular person but of a group of persons and of all those who have the responsibility at the two senior levels of government of meeting their share of the burden and of their responsibility in this matter. I believe that is the way to look at this situation, and not to seek to try and cause divisions at a time and in respect of a matter that can only move forward providing this spirit of co-operation exists.
That is what the people of Canada expect us to do in this matter, and I am sure that kind of motivation and consideration will give us the opportunity of realizing all the benefits of this measure much more readily and much more effectively. speechtext: Good. May I ask the minister another question. Does the minister realize that in this insistence upon six rather than five provinces he is really straining at a gnat? Does he realize that at the present time the five provinces which have agreed represent 56.3 per cent of the population of Canada. The government formula upon which it is so stubbornly insisting requires that one more province come into the scheme. That one more province could be Prince Edward Island, which would add six-tenths of 1 per cent to the population of the agreeing provinces. The percentage of the population of Canada represented by the provinces then agreeing would be 56.9 per cent instead of 56.3 per cent. Does the minister not think the government is really drawing it pretty fine to require that much by way of an addition?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
I have already dealt with that. I believe the requirement of six provinces is an important condition. Hon. members may not agree, and my hon. friend may not agree,

but what we are seeking is a nation-wide system. I am sure if we had not put in the condition that there be at least six provinces, we would not have had five.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: You have five now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: I know, but I say we would not have had five. I have every hope, every belief and every reason for being optimistic that there is no question but that we are going to get one more and more than one more province. I am sure that the condition of six has been correct, and I am sure time will prove that to be the case.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: The government has already modified its proposal by introducing legislation at this stage when there are only five; why not modify it further and be sensible?

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Am I clear on this one point? The minister intimated the other day that he hoped there would be six provinces shortly. Assuming that there is a sixth province, would it then follow that the province of Saskatchewan would be eligible to be qualified this year rather than having to wait until the beginning of 1959?

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: I have already explained that this afternoon. Under those conditions the answer is no.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: I think in answer to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre the minister said if there were six provinces which decided to participate in this program, and if the legislation had been proclaimed, then the province of Saskatchewan, which ten years ago introduced a program in good faith believing that it would be a program with which the Minister of National Health and Welfare would agree with; after having had that program for ten years, Saskatchewan should be able to qualify in 1957. May I ask the minister whether I am right in assuming that Saskatchewan would qualify as soon as six provinces pass legislation and have it proclaimed?

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: I cannot add anything to what I have said.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: If six provinces proclaim such legislation, is the federal government prepared to pay money to the provinces which have schemes in operation?

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: That is one of the conditions.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: I know it is. Has the minister had any assurance from any province other than Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia? I take it they would come in readily. In other words, has the minister assurance from either Ontario or Newfoundland that they will have an act proclaimed within a year?

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: No, I cannot say that. All the provinces and the federal government are now in the process of considering the terms of a draft master agreement, and negotiations are under way. The provinces that have expressed their concurrence are all doing their utmost to expedite matters as quickly as they can. I do not think I can add anything more at this time.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
We may not be back to where we started, but we are a considerable distance on the way back. If the minister is saying that six provinces must have schemes proclaimed this year in order for Saskatchewan to get money this year, and if the minister cannot give any assurance that there will be any law proclaimed in any province other than Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, it is then obvious to everyone that there will be no money in 1957 for the provinces, some of which have had schemes in operation for many years.
I think that attitude of the government is wrong and shortsighted; that the government should now say, in 1957, that they are prepared to pay money from the national treasury to any province which has a plan in operation. I am sure that would not detract from the spirit of co-operation across the country, but would be a solid indication to the people of this nation that this government really means business now.
